items.title: 1. The clinical map: three overlapping problems
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 1.1 Think in terms of disease, operation and rescue

Set 18 contains three intersecting tasks:

- (i) recognise patients whose systemic condition changes anaesthetic risk (diabetes, obesity, adrenal/thyroid disease, autoimmune disease, frailty, post-transplant state).
- (ii) understand surgical requirements from diagnostic hysteroscopy to robot-assisted pelvic exenteration.
- (iii) prevent, recognise and manage organ-specific complications (sepsis, bleeding, distension-media absorption, catecholamine crisis, graft hypoperfusion, severe endocrine or oncological emergency).

- The best viva approach starts with **what must happen technically**, then maps the physiology and patient reserve to induction, the critical operative phase, emergence and postoperative surveillance.

**A practical preoperative briefing asks:**

- What will be resected or reconstructed?
- What site and duration?
- Is the patient at risk of aspirating?
- Is access to the airway restricted after draping or robotic docking?
- Is CO₂ insufflation used?
- What position (steep Trendelenburg, lithotomy, lateral or prone)?
- Will large amounts of irrigation fluid or contrast be used?
- Could bleeding be occult (retroperitoneal, pelvic, renal)?
- Is renal function impaired or threatened?
- Are there endocrine triggers (tumour manipulation, fasting, stress, interruption of steroids or insulin)?
- What is the rescue plan if the case converts to major surgery?

## 1.2 The shared perioperative sequence

**Preoperative:**

- Confirm urgency, consent/capacity and alternative treatments; identify active infection, haemorrhage, endocrine crisis, unstable cardiovascular/respiratory disease and frailty.
- Evaluate baseline fluid and electrolyte status, Hb/coagulation, kidney function, glucose/ketones, relevant drugs (insulin, SGLT2i, GLP-1, steroids, immunosuppression, anticoagulants), aspiration/airway and the planned postoperative location.
- Correct what changes outcome without unnecessarily delaying urgent source control.

**Intraoperative:**

- Select a technique that meets requirements for immobilisation, airway control and position
- Confirm access/monitoring before docking or lithotomy
- Assess fluid responsiveness and tolerance, blood loss, perfusion and temperatures
- Prevent pressure/nerve injury
- Treat haemodynamic changes by mechanism
- Know the critical step at which clamping, reperfusion, irrigation or tumour manipulation can precipitate collapse.

- **Postoperative:** hand over operation, blood loss and actual fluids/irrigant deficit, urine output and interpretation, pathology-specific complications, devices/catheters/drains, analgesic plan, anticoagulant restart and observation triggers. Good care is defined by graft/renal, neurological, respiratory and wound outcomes—not just a normal PACU blood pressure.

## 1.3 Elective versus emergency surgery: the same operation is not the same anaesthetic

- Elective ureteroscopy in a stable patient may require only brief GA or carefully selected sedation.
- Emergency ureteroscopy with an infected obstructed collecting system is a **sepsis source-control procedure** with a full-stomach possibility, vasoplegia, bacteraemia when the system is pressurised and risk of postoperative ICU.
- Diagnostic laparoscopy for infertility is different from laparoscopy for ruptured ectopic pregnancy.
- An emergency gastroscopy in a patient vomiting blood is different from screening colonoscopy.
- In every acute case, resuscitation and correction of severe potassium/acidosis/glucose problems occur **in parallel** with arranging definitive intervention; a preinduction normal MAP may be entirely catecholamine-dependent.

items.title: 2. Diabetes: a metabolic and autonomic disease, not just a glucose result
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 2.1 Pathophysiology and why surgical patients deteriorate

- Insulin deficiency (type 1 absolute; type 2 relative/variable) causes impaired peripheral glucose use, increased hepatic gluconeogenesis and lipolysis.
- Surgical stress releases catecholamines, cortisol, glucagon and growth hormone, increasing insulin resistance and hepatic glucose production.
- Hyperglycaemia impairs neutrophil function, increases infection and wound complications, produces osmotic diuresis and contributes to endothelial dysfunction.
- **Hypoglycaemia** causes neuroglycopenia and arrhythmia and may be entirely masked by GA.
- **Ketoacidosis** results from insulin deficiency and unchecked ketogenesis; it can occur with only modest glucose elevation during SGLT2 inhibitor therapy.
- Intensive normoglycaemic regimens increase severe hypoglycaemia without reliably improving outcome [R1–R3].

- Diabetes carries macrovascular disease (CAD, stroke, peripheral disease), nephropathy (CKD, potassium disorders, altered drug excretion), retinopathy, neuropathy and autonomic dysfunction.
- Some patients have limited exercise capacity because of PAD, not a directly measurable cardiac MET value; risk assessment must account for the reason.
- Obesity and OSA often coexist; gastroparesis alters aspiration risk even after conventional fasting.
- Infection, dehydration and missed insulin can precipitate DKA or HHS.
- Diabetes also worsens perioperative foot/pressure injuries, particularly during prolonged lithotomy.

## 2.2 How to assess diabetic autonomic neuropathy: an examinable distinction

- Ask about **orthostatic dizziness/syncope**, impaired exercise HR response, resting tachycardia, silent myocardial ischaemia, sweating abnormalities/heat intolerance, gastroparesis (early satiety, bloating, vomiting), constipation/diarrhoea, urinary retention, erectile dysfunction and hypoglycaemia unawareness.
- Examine supine and standing BP/HR (the BP may fall without appropriate tachycardia), resting pulse and rhythm, peripheral neuropathy and signs of organ disease.
- Bedside cardiovascular autonomic tests can include deep-breathing HR variability, Valsalva ratio and lying-to-standing HR response, interpreted with age, medications and rhythm.
- Formal autonomic testing is not required for every case.

**Anaesthetic implications:**

- Inability to increase HR when BP falls
- Severe induction/neuraxial hypotension despite a deceptively normal resting BP
- Exaggerated response to exogenous vasoactive drugs
- Greater gastroparesis/aspiration risk
- Less reliable warning symptoms of MI or hypoglycaemia
- Increased urinary retention and postoperative haemodynamic lability.
- Have a direct-acting vasopressor ready, maintain assessed filling, use appropriate aspiration precautions and consider invasive monitoring in severe disease/major operations.
- Avoid assuming every tachycardic patient has anxiety or every hypotensive patient needs 2 L fluid.

## 2.3 Preoperative diabetes assessment and decisions

- Document type/duration, recent HbA1c and capillary/CGM pattern, severe hypoglycaemia and DKA history, pump/closed-loop settings, basal and bolus regimen, last doses, ketones if unwell or SGLT2-exposed, renal function, potassium, cardiovascular symptoms, neuropathy/foot status and infection.
- HbA1c gauges medium-term control but does not tell you today’s safety; anaemia, CKD and haemoglobinopathies can alter interpretation.
- Elective surgery should be postponed for DKA/HHS or serious untreated metabolic derangement, and optimisation considered for markedly uncontrolled disease, but no single HbA1c threshold is an absolute surgical ban.
- Arrange the first list if possible and limit unnecessary fasting.

| **Therapy** | **Perioperative principle** | **Risk and practical caveat** |
|---|---|---|
| **Type 1 basal insulin** | **Never omit entirely**; continue reduced or adjusted basal/IV insulin with dextrose as needed | Omission causes ketosis even when fasting; pump interruption needs an alternative immediately |
| Long-acting basal insulin | Frequently 75–80% of usual dose near fasting for selected patients; individualise regimen | Elderly, CKD and prior fasting hypos often require greater adjustment |
| Prandial/rapid insulin | Omit a scheduled meal bolus when meal omitted; provide correction or IV insulin if needed | Do not omit essential insulin in a ketotic patient |
| Metformin | Many hospital pathways hold on day of surgery, particularly renal injury/contrast/major illness; some guidelines permit continuation in selected cases | Lactic acidosis risk depends on illness, renal function and hypoperfusion rather than metformin alone |
| Sulfonylurea | Usually omit on fasting day | Prolonged hypoglycaemia, especially CKD |
| **SGLT2 inhibitor** | Australian/ACC/ADA-style pathway: stop ≥3 days before elective surgery (ertugliflozin ≥4); check ketones if emergency/unwell | Euglycaemic ketoacidosis; UK 2025 consensus instead recommends omit day before/day of surgery plus risk mitigation. **Follow local policy and explain difference** [R1–R3] |
| GLP-1 / dual GIP–GLP-1 | Risk stratify for GI symptoms, dose escalation, suspected gastric retention; most patients need not automatically stop therapy | Delayed emptying and aspiration risk in selected symptomatic/high-risk patients; recent multi-society recommendations favour individualisation |
| Insulin pump/CGM | Clarify whether pump can stay on for short accessible procedures; who manages it, alarms, site/diathermy and backup | CGM can lag/under-read; capillary/venous glucose remains necessary intraoperatively |

- For small procedures with predictable fasting, a modified usual regimen and monitored correction may suffice.
- For **major surgery, prolonged fasting, unstable insulin-controlled diabetes or emergency metabolic stress**, use an institutionally approved variable-rate IV insulin infusion (VRIII) with appropriate glucose-containing substrate and potassium guided by renal status.
- Do not simply run insulin without a dextrose source or omit basal requirements in type 1 diabetes.
- Distinguish VRIII (control around fasting/surgery) from a DKA insulin/fluid/electrolyte protocol (correct acidosis/ketogenesis and replace profound deficits).
- Check glucose at least hourly on IV insulin and more frequently during instability, plus serial K/ketones/ABG as required.
- A practical perioperative glucose range is around **5.6–10 mmol/L** where achievable without hypoglycaemia, with some acute-care pathways accepting up to 12 mmol/L transiently; avoid aggressive attempts at tight normal glucose. [R1–R3]

## 2.4 A real danger: euglycaemic DKA after SGLT2 inhibition

- SGLT2 inhibition causes glycosuria and lowers circulating insulin requirements, favouring glucagon-driven lipolysis/ketogenesis.
- Fasting, infection, surgery, low-carbohydrate diets, insulin omission and dehydration amplify this.
- Presentation may be nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, tachypnoea, malaise or shock with **high-anion-gap acidosis, raised blood β-hydroxybutyrate and glucose that may be near normal**.
- A routine glucose reading cannot exclude it.
- In an emergency operation, stop SGLT2 inhibitor, obtain blood ketones, pH, bicarbonate, anion gap and electrolytes; treat euglycaemic DKA using insulin and **earlier dextrose substrate** than classic very-high-glucose DKA, potassium and cautious fluid/renal management with senior/endocrine support.
- Continue until ketosis and acidosis resolve, not merely until glucose is normal. [R1,R2]

## 2.5 Intraoperative and postoperative diabetic management

- Priorities are avoiding hypoglycaemia, marked hyperglycaemia, ketogenesis and organ hypoperfusion.
- Maintain oxygenation, normothermia and appropriate antibiotics; control infection and pain rather than using insulin to conceal an uncontrolled stress response.
- Check blood glucose regularly, reassess potassium if insulin or major fluid shifts occur and treat critical values according to institutional algorithms.
- Steroids raise glucose needs, but an indicated stress steroid dose should not be withheld in an adrenal crisis.
- The emergence area must know the last insulin, next basal dose, oral intake plan and who is responsible for monitoring.
- Restart oral drugs only when eating, haemodynamically stable and kidney function appropriate; **do not restart SGLT2i in an actively fasting, ketotic or unwell patient**.
- For insulin pump users, document how and when transition back occurs.
- Postoperative AKI, delayed gastric emptying, infection, pressure wounds, myocardial injury and hypoglycaemia warrant active surveillance.

## 2.6 Practical perioperative insulin and hyperglycaemic emergencies

- **The examination decision is whether the patient can safely fast without losing basal insulin.** For type 1 diabetes, subcutaneous basal insulin must continue in an appropriate reduced/modified dose or be replaced by IV insulin; correction-only insulin is unsafe because ketogenesis can occur even when glucose is not very high.
- For short procedures with one missed meal and stable control, an institutionally approved adjusted basal–bolus or pump plan may be reasonable.
- For prolonged fasting, major surgery, poor control or an emergency, plan IV insulin with glucose-containing substrate, frequent blood glucose and potassium assessment, and an explicit transition back to usual insulin with overlap to avoid rebound ketosis.
- The 2026 Association of Anaesthetists/JBDS consensus recommends a documented individual plan, hourly capillary glucose while receiving variable-rate IV insulin, and different glucose targets according to diabetic therapy [R22].
- A continuous glucose monitor or closed-loop pump is not automatically reliable or safely managed during GA: consider electrocautery, pressure/poor perfusion, imaging, whether the device remains accessible and whether the responsible team can adjust it; confirm treatment decisions with capillary/arterial samples.

**Drug-specific planning:**

- Sulfonylureas/meglitinides can cause fasting hypoglycaemia and are commonly omitted on the morning of surgery
- Metformin decisions depend on renal function, contrast, illness and local policy rather than a universal instruction
- GLP-1 receptor agonists require symptom-based aspiration assessment rather than routine assumption of gastric retention.
- If on an SGLT2 inhibitor, document the last dose, evaluate illness/fasting and check capillary ketones if symptoms, acidosis or unexplained tachypnoea emerge even with normal glucose.
- Avoid restarting an SGLT2 inhibitor while ketotic, fasting, haemodynamically unstable or markedly unwell.

**Differentiate DKA, HHS and isolated stress hyperglycaemia:**

- DKA involves ketonaemia with metabolic acidosis and requires isotonic/balanced IV fluids according to volume/renal function, fixed-rate insulin and potassium replacement/monitoring under a DKA protocol.
- HHS involves marked hyperosmolality and dehydration, often in older type 2 diabetes, and requires careful gradual correction and search for the trigger; rapid tonicity shifts are dangerous.
- Stress hyperglycaemia without acidosis is managed with monitored insulin according to the operative setting.
- In both crises, treat infection/MI/other triggers and defer elective surgery.
- Persistent acidosis after glucose normalises is not evidence that DKA has resolved; confirm falling ketones and closure of the metabolic disturbance.

- **Postoperative handover:** identify the prescribed meal plan, when to restart basal and prandial insulin, when to stop IV insulin (with safe overlap), renal-function or steroid-dose changes, hypoglycaemia rescue and ketone-trigger thresholds. The first meal is a clinical transition point, not simply a discharge milestone.

items.title: 3. Obesity and respiratory reserve: induction, surgery and extubation all matter
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 3.1 Why oxygenation fails quickly

- Obesity reduces chest-wall compliance and **functional residual capacity (FRC)**; under GA, supine positioning and pneumoperitoneum can make FRC fall below closing capacity, causing rapid atelectasis, shunt and reduced safe apnoea time.
- Respiratory oxygen consumption is increased, the oxygen reservoir is proportionally smaller and mask ventilation may be difficult.
- OSA causes upper-airway collapsibility; obesity hypoventilation syndrome (OHS) adds awake hypercapnia, hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension and possible RV failure.
- Obesity also increases reflux, difficult IV/arterial access, VTE, wound complications, positional injury and altered drug pharmacokinetics.
- **BMI alone is an imperfect predictor of difficult intubation:** neck circumference, limited jaw/neck movement, airway history and obstructive physiology matter. [R4]

## 3.2 Preoperative obesity assessment

- History: exercise tolerance and the cause of limitation, witnessed apnoeas/snoring, CPAP/NIV adherence, daytime somnolence, resting SpO₂, bicarbonate/hypercapnia, prior difficult mask or intubation, severe reflux, previous bariatric surgery, pulmonary hypertension, CAD/HF, diabetes, VTE and GLP-1 symptoms.
- Consider STOP-Bang as a risk prompt rather than a diagnosis.
- Suspect OHS when awake hypercapnia, sustained low SpO₂ or raised bicarbonate suggests chronic hypoventilation; ABG if it will change management.
- Check BP with an appropriately sized cuff; in severe obesity, poorly fitting oscillometric cuffs can be inaccurate.
- Discuss the practicality and potential failure modes of radial invasive pressure monitoring when the procedure/physiology justify it.
- Assess bed/table weight and width, transfer aids and recovery CPAP availability.

## 3.3 Airway and ventilation: before, during and after

- The 2025 Society for Obesity and Bariatric Anaesthesia recommendations prioritise **ramped ≥30° head-up preoxygenation**, planned rescue, video laryngoscopy as first-line for many patients, apnoeic oxygenation when useful, and **awake, head-up extubation after quantitative neuromuscular reversal** [R4].
- Ramping aligns ear and sternal notch and improves FRC and airway access.
- Consider CPAP/NIV preoxygenation when obstruction/atelectasis is marked.
- For detailed physiology read BJA Education [R17]; a rapid sequence approach may be indicated for actual aspiration risk, but obesity alone does not mean every patient has a full stomach.
- Plan rescue and access to a supraglottic airway and emergency front-of-neck access.

- Ventilate with **6–8 mL/kg predicted body weight**, not total body weight; adjust PEEP/recruitment to oxygenation and circulatory tolerance.
- Pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg worsen compliance and raise airway pressures; check ETT position after positioning and increase minute ventilation as CO₂ absorption rises.
- Beware increases in intra-abdominal/thoracic pressure worsening venous return and RV load.
- Drug dosing uses drug-specific scalars (total, ideal, lean or adjusted body weight) rather than one universal weight; monitor response and quantitative NM block.
- Multimodal analgesia, avoidance of unnecessarily sedating opioid/gabapentinoid combinations, PONV prophylaxis and early mobilisation reduce respiratory and VTE burden.

**Extubation is an independent high-risk event:**

- Allow head-up re-expansion, normothermia, reversal and return to cooperative protective reflexes; inspect facial/tongue swelling after prolonged Trendelenburg.
- A normal SpO₂ under oxygen can conceal hypoventilation.
- Resume home CPAP/NIV early, provide monitored postoperative care for OHS/high opioid exposure, encourage early mobilisation and plan VTE prophylaxis appropriate to risk and bleeding.

## 3.4 Obesity: drug selection, OSA/OHS and recovery decisions

**Assess obesity-related physiology rather than BMI alone:**

- Evaluate STOP-Bang or known OSA, CPAP adherence, possible obesity hypoventilation (daytime hypercapnia or raised bicarbonate), reflux and previous aspiration, cardiopulmonary disease, pulmonary hypertension, positioning limits, reduced functional reserve and difficult IV access.
- The patient with OHS and resting hypercapnia may require preoperative gas analysis and a higher-dependency postoperative plan; simply prescribing extra oxygen can mask hypoventilation.
- Assess ramping, equipment/operating table limits, bariatric lifting, pressure injury prevention, appropriate cuff size and whether emergency front-of-neck airway access is realistically possible.

**Airway sequence:**

- Preoxygenate in head-up/ramped position with tight-mask technique, consider CPAP/NIV or high-flow oxygen where appropriate, use video laryngoscopy with the tube and rescue devices available, and minimise unprotected apnoea.
- Obesity alone does not mandate RSI, but active reflux, bowel obstruction, marked gastroparesis or other aspiration factors may.
- Dose hypnotics/opioids and muscle relaxants to drug-specific pharmacokinetic scalars rather than treating total, ideal and lean body weight as interchangeable.
- Avoid residual neuromuscular block: use quantitative monitoring and complete reversal.
- Lung-protective tidal volumes are based on predicted/ideal body weight; adapt PEEP and recruitment to oxygenation and haemodynamics, particularly during pneumoperitoneum and Trendelenburg.

**Recovery is a second airway procedure:**

- Extubate fully awake, head-up, with neuromuscular recovery confirmed and a plan for reintubation.
- Resume the patient's CPAP early when appropriate and prescribe multimodal opioid-sparing analgesia without allowing untreated pain or excessive sedatives to compromise ventilation.
- Escalate for persistent hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, obstructive events or recurrent apnoea and consider monitored overnight care.
- The 2025 SOBA recommendations emphasise airway planning, head-up oxygenation and a specific extubation strategy [R4].

items.title: 4. Adrenal insufficiency and steroid dependence
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 4.1 Primary, secondary and iatrogenic insufficiency

- **Primary adrenal insufficiency** (e.g. autoimmune Addison disease or bilateral adrenal destruction) reduces cortisol **and often aldosterone**, producing hypovolaemia, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia and low vascular catecholamine responsiveness.
- **Secondary/tertiary insufficiency** from pituitary/hypothalamic disease or chronic glucocorticoids reduces cortisol but often preserves mineralocorticoid function, so marked hyperkalaemia is less typical.
- Chronic steroids suppress ACTH and adrenal response; risk depends on dose, duration, route, recent withdrawal and intercurrent illness.
- Patients may also have diabetes, osteoporosis, skin fragility and infection risk from treatment.

- The stress response to surgery should increase cortisol availability; patients without sufficient reserve may develop **refractory hypotension, weakness, nausea/vomiting, abdominal pain, fever, confusion, hypoglycaemia and hyponatraemia**, sometimes mimicking septic shock or gastrointestinal catastrophe.
- Do not wait for laboratory confirmation in suspected adrenal crisis.
- Cortisol sampling/ACTH testing may help later but must not delay treatment. [R5]

## 4.2 Preoperative and intraoperative decisions

- Identify diagnostic basis, maintenance hydrocortisone/prednisone, mineralocorticoid replacement, stress sick-day instructions, emergency steroid kit and last actual dose.
- Assess volume status, Na/K/glucose, active infection and hypotension.
- **Continue the patient’s ordinary steroid replacement** and provide stress coverage when indicated.
- For substantial major stress or established Addison disease under GA, a widely used 2024 ESE/Endocrine Society regimen is **hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction then 200 mg over 24 h (or 50 mg IV every 6 h)**, with ongoing IV therapy while severely ill/unable to take oral medication, then step down according to clinical recovery.
- Some local low/intermediate-stress protocols prescribe smaller supplements; do not present the major-stress regimen as universally necessary for every 10-minute minor local procedure.
- Mineralocorticoid substitution usually continues once eating; high-dose hydrocortisone temporarily provides some mineralocorticoid effect. [R5]

- Adrenal crisis: immediate hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM, **rapid isotonic resuscitation adjusted to heart/renal function**, dextrose for hypoglycaemia, potassium/ECG treatment when needed, treat sepsis or other precipitant and use vasopressors if shock persists.
- Cortisol deficiency reduces alpha-adrenoceptor response; pressure may not normalise with vasopressor alone.
- Monitor urine, glucose, electrolytes and lactate.
- After surgery, ensure a **written transition back to oral steroids** as GI recovery permits; avoid abrupt cessation.
- Refractory unexplained vasodilatory shock in a steroid-dependent patient should trigger this differential even if a routine steroid chart exists.

## 4.3 Adrenal insufficiency: assessment, stress coverage and rescue

**Identify who is genuinely at risk:**

- Primary Addison disease causes both glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid deficiency (hypotension, salt loss, hyperkalaemia); secondary/tertiary suppression preserves aldosterone more often but can still produce adrenal crisis under surgical stress.
- Ask about systemic steroid dose, route, duration, recent cessation, repeated injections and current adrenal testing; inhaled/topical preparations can contribute to suppression at high cumulative exposure.
- Look for weight loss, postural symptoms, nausea, pigmentation (primary disease), hyponatraemia, hypoglycaemia and reduced stress tolerance.
- If risk is uncertain in an elective patient, discuss 8–9 AM cortisol/ACTH stimulation testing with endocrinology rather than treating a single random cortisol as decisive.

**Management differs by surgery and established replacement:**

- Continue normal steroid therapy when feasible; give supplementary parenteral hydrocortisone for patients with established adrenal insufficiency undergoing significant surgery or unable to take oral medication.
- A commonly taught major-stress regimen is hydrocortisone 100 mg IV at induction followed by 200 mg over 24 h (or 50 mg IV every 6 h), then taper promptly to oral replacement as illness resolves [R5].
- This is an example aligned with major-stress guidance, not a universal dose for every minor dental or day-case procedure: less invasive procedures may use smaller coverage under a documented local endocrine protocol.
- Monitor blood glucose, potassium, sodium, fluid status and infection.
- In primary Addison disease, resume mineralocorticoid as the patient returns to maintenance dosing; high-dose hydrocortisone supplies temporary mineralocorticoid activity.

**Adrenal crisis:**

- Suspect it with refractory hypotension (especially vasopressor-resistant), altered consciousness, hypoglycaemia, vomiting/abdominal pain and electrolyte disturbance in an at-risk patient.
- Draw cortisol/ACTH if practicable but never delay treatment.
- Give hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM immediately, resuscitate with assessed isotonic fluid and glucose where indicated, treat infection/bleeding and follow with 200 mg hydrocortisone/24 h, monitoring sodium and potassium.
- Do not assume every hypotensive patient on steroids has crisis: haemorrhage, anaphylaxis, cardiogenic causes and sepsis need simultaneous evaluation.
- The 2021.2 Addison-related SAQ specifically makes pre/intra/postoperative management rather than steroid dose alone important.

items.title: 5. Phaeochromocytoma: a high-stakes endocrine anaesthetic
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 5.1 Understand the haemodynamic phases

- Phaeochromocytomas are catecholamine-producing tumours of adrenal chromaffin cells; extra-adrenal sympathetic paragangliomas may behave similarly.
- Noradrenaline-driven alpha vasoconstriction, adrenaline-associated tachyarrhythmia and beta effects, and fluctuating tumour release explain **paroxysmal headache, sweating, palpitations, hypertension, orthostatic symptoms, glucose intolerance and cardiomyopathy**.
- Some tumours are biochemically active without classic symptoms.
- Tumour compression, insufflation, laryngoscopy, pain and certain medications may cause massive discharge.
- In contrast, chronic vasoconstriction contracts effective plasma volume, and abrupt catecholamine withdrawal after **adrenal vein ligation** produces profound vasodilation and hypotension.
- The answer must separate these phases rather than applying one generic antihypertensive plan.

![Mechanism-based haemodynamic trajectory during phaeochromocytoma resection](set18-fig1.png)

Mechanism-based haemodynamic trajectory during phaeochromocytoma resection

## 5.2 Preoperative investigations and optimisation (high-priority SAQ)

- **Confirm biochemical diagnosis** with plasma free metanephrines or 24-h fractionated urinary metanephrines under suitable collection conditions.
- Plasma sampling ideally follows appropriate rest/posture and attention to medications, stress and renal impairment; an isolated modest elevation is not definitive.
- CT/MRI locates lesion and evaluates bilateral/multifocal disease; assess genetic/family associations (MEN2, VHL, NF1, SDHx) and possible associated thyroid medullary carcinoma or contralateral adrenal disease.
- ECG and TTE investigate catecholamine cardiomyopathy, LVH, dysrhythmia and dynamic function; troponin/BNP as indicated.
- Check glucose/HbA1c, renal function, potassium, Hb, orthostatic BP and intravascular depletion.
- Anaesthetist, endocrinology and surgeon should agree blood products, vascular access, operative approach, expected clamp/ligation time and emergency pathways. [R6,R7]

**Alpha blockade comes before beta blockade:**

- Phenoxybenzamine (nonselective irreversible alpha blockade) or doxazosin (selective reversible alpha-1) is titrated over roughly 1–2 weeks, with monitoring of seated and standing BP and symptoms.
- Typical goals are controlled BP without severe postural collapse, reduced spells and enough venous capacity to re-expand the circulation.
- Adequate salt/fluid intake and cautious volume expansion are often used where cardiac function permits; overfilling a catecholamine cardiomyopathy is harmful.
- Beta blockade may then address persistent tachycardia, **never started alone in uncontrolled alpha-mediated vasoconstriction**.
- Calcium channel blockers and metyrosine are adjuncts in selected cases.
- PRESCRIPT found no difference in time outside BP targets between phenoxybenzamine and doxazosin, although secondary haemodynamic instability favoured phenoxybenzamine; no meaningful clinical outcome superiority was established [T1].

**Preinduction plan:**

- Reliable arterial line (often awake), two good peripheral IVs, infusion pumps and ready short-acting vasodilator (nicardipine/clevidipine or nitroprusside in suitable setting), beta blocker (esmolol for rate after alpha control), magnesium where useful and direct vasopressor (noradrenaline/vasopressin) already prepared.
- Central access/CO monitoring or TEE is based on anticipated instability or ventricular disease, not automatic for every small adrenalectomy.
- Avoid unnecessary sympathetic stimuli; smooth induction and intubation, adequate analgesia/paralysis and good communication with surgeon.
- Metoclopramide, glucagon, indirect sympathomimetics (ephedrine) and drugs causing marked catecholamine release should be avoided or selected only with specialist justification.
- In a patient with possible combined adrenal insufficiency, coordinate steroid timing with endocrinology because glucocorticoids can stimulate catecholamine release in an untreated functional tumour, yet proven adrenal crisis still requires treatment. [R7]

## 5.3 Intraoperative sequence and three different types of hypotension/hypertension

**Before vascular control:**

- Insufflation and tumour handling may cause extreme hypertension, tachycardia, dysrhythmia and myocardial ischaemia.
- First ask surgeon to pause manipulation, deepen anaesthesia/analgesia and assess ventilation/CO₂; titrate rapid vasodilation and rate control while avoiding excessive hypotension.
- Intraoperative hypotension before ligation may be anaesthetic vasodilation plus alpha blockade, true hypovolaemia, bleeding or depressed LV function: assess echo/CO, blood loss and dynamic response; do not assume every low pressure means an alpha-blocked patient should receive litres of saline.

**At adrenal vein ligation:**

- Sudden fall in circulating catecholamines, pre-existing vasodilator and alpha-blockade effects, relative hypovolaemia and possibly myocardial stunning cause profound low SVR and hypotension.
- Withdraw antihypertensives, treat with titrated direct-acting vasopressors (noradrenaline ± vasopressin), restore demonstrable volume deficits and investigate haemorrhage or myocardial dysfunction.
- If low cardiac output persists with ventricular dysfunction, a tailored inotrope/CO strategy is required.
- Check glucose: removal of catecholamine-driven inhibition of insulin can cause **post-resection hypoglycaemia**. [R6,R7]

**At emergence/postoperative period:**

- Hypertension may recur from pain, agitation or residual tumour/other causes; hypotension can persist with vasoplegia; hypoglycaemia, adrenal insufficiency (especially bilateral adrenal surgery), AKI, arrhythmia and cardiomyopathy remain relevant.
- Observe high-risk cases in HDU/ICU.
- Confirm postoperative biochemical surveillance and referral for genetic/endocrine follow-up.
- A stable arterial pressure does not exclude ongoing low output.

**Worked oral exam:**

- A patient under GA for laparoscopic phaeochromocytoma resection develops BP 220/110 and HR 150 during dissection.
- Immediately ask surgeon to stop manipulating tumour, confirm ECG rhythm/anaesthetic depth/ETCO₂, treat sympathetic activation with a titratable arterial vasodilator and rate control, assess ischaemia and avoid reflex fluids.
- Ten minutes later after vein ligation, MAP falls to 45: stop vasodilator, assess bleeding/ventricular function, use direct vasopressor and small tested volume/blood, check glucose and ABG.
- The same patient needs opposite haemodynamic treatment at different surgical phases.

## 5.4 Unstable phaeochromocytoma: a phase-based differential and rescue

**Before induction:**

- Verify actual alpha blockade, volume restoration and reversible catecholamine cardiomyopathy rather than counting days of therapy.
- Phenoxybenzamine is irreversible/non-selective and can cause prolonged post-resection hypotension; doxazosin is selective/reversible, with potentially less persistent blockade.
- Start beta blockade only after adequate alpha blockade if required for tachyarrhythmia.
- Consider echocardiography with heart-failure features; separate tumour secretion from medication-induced orthostasis or inadequate preload.
- Prepare arterial monitoring (often before induction), two robust IV lines, a plan for rapid-acting vasodilators and vasopressors, and communication about every tumour-handling step.

**At intubation or insufflation, hypertension and tachycardia:**

- Check depth/analgesia, hypercarbia, bladder distension, tumour manipulation and medication error.
- If catecholamine-driven, pause manipulation, deepen anaesthesia and titrate short-acting vasodilation (e.g. phentolamine or nicardipine; nitroprusside in suitable expert settings), treating tachyarrhythmia with a short beta-blocker only when alpha blockade/afterload management is adequate.
- Persistent severe BP rise increases risk of cerebral haemorrhage, pulmonary oedema, myocardial ischaemia and dissection.
- New ST changes, falling ETCO₂, pulmonary oedema or global hypokinesis may signal catecholamine cardiomyopathy, not merely inadequate anaesthetic depth.

**After adrenal vein ligation or tumour removal, hypotension:**

- Catecholamines fall suddenly while alpha-blockade and anaesthetic vasodilation persist; surgical bleeding and chronic contracted intravascular volume compound the problem.
- Stop vasodilators, check surgical field and Hb, reassess cardiac output with echo where needed, give small targeted volume if responsive and initiate noradrenaline or selected vasopressin support.
- If persistent low output, distinguish cardiogenic shock from distributive/relative hypovolaemia before inotropy.
- Monitor for severe hypoglycaemia caused by rebound insulin release, plus postoperative hypertension from residual tumour or pain.
- Some adrenalectomy patients also need glucocorticoid assessment depending on bilateral surgery/underlying pathology.
- The 2026.1 examiner stem asks for potential causes of haemodynamic instability: an answer limited to catecholamine release misses insufflation, haemorrhage, low-output cardiomyopathy, drug effects and post-ligation vasoplegia.

## 5.5 Adrenalectomy beyond phaeochromocytoma

**Do not assume every adrenal mass secretes catecholamines:**

- Determine whether the patient has cortisol excess (Cushing syndrome), primary aldosteronism (Conn syndrome), a functional phaeochromocytoma, adrenocortical carcinoma, metastasis or a non-functional incidentaloma.
- Confirm endocrine assessment before adrenal surgery, including exclusion of catecholamine excess when clinically appropriate; a supposedly non-functional mass with an undiagnosed phaeochromocytoma can make induction catastrophic.
- Laparoscopic unilateral adrenalectomy often shares the pneumoperitoneum/positioning issues of other laparoscopy, but dissection close to renal vein/IVC or major vessels may cause rapid haemorrhage.
- Open surgery may be required for large invasive carcinoma.

**Cortisol excess:**

- Assess diabetes, hypertension, obesity, OSA, infection vulnerability, skin fragility, difficult venous access, muscle weakness, osteoporosis and high VTE risk.
- Chronic hypercortisolism suppresses the contralateral adrenal axis; postoperative glucocorticoid replacement and monitoring for adrenal insufficiency must be coordinated with endocrinology.
- **Primary aldosteronism:** identify uncontrolled hypertension, hypokalaemia/metabolic alkalosis, arrhythmia risk and renal adaptations; optimise potassium and blood pressure (e.g. mineralocorticoid-receptor antagonist when appropriate) and reassess potassium/renal function after removal because transient hypoaldosteronism and hyperkalaemia may occur.
- **Bilateral adrenalectomy:** causes permanent adrenal insufficiency, requiring ongoing glucocorticoid and mineralocorticoid replacement and crisis education.
- **Operative fluid/analgesia:** use balanced fluid and blood replacement guided by real losses, titrated vasopressor for appropriate physiology, multimodal analgesia and incision-specific truncal blocks or neuraxial techniques where appropriate; avoid indiscriminate fluid loading for hypotension that may instead reflect vasodilation, bleeding or steroid insufficiency.

items.title: 6. Carcinoid tumours, carcinoid syndrome and crisis
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 6.1 Mechanism and preoperative recognition

- Neuroendocrine tumours may secrete serotonin and other vasoactive mediators.
- Clinical carcinoid syndrome—often flushing, secretory diarrhoea, bronchospasm and haemodynamic disturbance—most often occurs with hormone release into systemic circulation, frequently when hepatic metabolism is bypassed by liver metastases.
- Serotonin-associated endocardial fibrosis preferentially damages right-sided valves (tricuspid regurgitation/stenosis, pulmonary valve disease); left-sided disease is less typical unless there is a shunt or bronchial primary.
- Carcinoid heart disease changes anaesthesia through RV dysfunction and fixed valvular constraints.
- Chronic diarrhoea causes dehydration, electrolyte loss, malnutrition and vitamin deficiency; bronchospasm and labile vasomotor tone reduce reserve. [R8]

- Ask specifically about flushing, diarrhoea, wheeze, prior crises, functional capacity, syncope, volume loss and somatostatin therapy.
- Use 24-h urinary 5-HIAA or other appropriate serotonin markers, imaging and multidisciplinary NET assessment to characterise activity.
- **Obtain echocardiography in clinical or biochemical carcinoid syndrome** to assess RV and valve function.
- Evaluate electrolytes, renal function, anaemia, nutrition and anticoagulants; plan for major tumour and liver bleeding if extensive resection.
- Correct depletion and decide on postoperative HDU/ICU based on RV disease, surgical magnitude and active symptoms.

## 6.2 Intraoperative crisis: update older octreotide-first teaching

- Carcinoid crisis is sudden severe haemodynamic instability, often profound vasodilation/hypotension but sometimes hypertension, during tumour manipulation, induction or other stress.
- Exclude haemorrhage, anaesthetic effect, anaphylaxis, acute RV failure, sepsis and CO₂-related events.
- Reduce triggering manipulation and protect ventilation, oxygenation, temperature and volume status.

**Important 2026 evidence update:**

- An international 44-expert consensus found **routine prophylactic IV short-acting octreotide unnecessary**, and recommends **vasopressors first line** (noradrenaline, phenylephrine or vasopressin as appropriate); short-acting octreotide can be an **adjunct**, not a treatment whose preparation should delay vasopressor support.
- Established long-acting somatostatin therapy can continue for disease control.
- Traditional prohibitions against all catecholamines or all histamine-releasing anaesthetic drugs are not evidence-based absolute rules; select drug by cardiac physiology and monitor response.
- If the RV is failing, a carefully selected inotrope and management of PVR may be necessary. [R8]

- A useful sequence: alert surgeon and ask to pause tumour manipulation → verify airway, oxygenation, ECG and depth → exclude bleeding/anaphylaxis/embolism with rapid assessment → vasopressor promptly for low SVR → assessed fluid if depleted rather than automatic large bolus → echo for carcinoid valve/RV disease → octreotide adjunct if persistent crisis in specialist pathway.
- Continue appropriate multimodal analgesia to reduce stress.
- Postoperatively, monitor haemodynamics, heart failure, bronchospasm, electrolyte losses and recurrent crisis, especially with active syndrome.
- The historical ‘octreotide for everyone and avoid any catecholamine’ answer is no longer robust.

## 6.3 Carcinoid resection: operation-specific plan and haemodynamic reasoning

**Preoperative:**

- Determine whether the tumour is associated with true carcinoid syndrome (flushing, diarrhoea, wheeze), malnutrition/dehydration, metastatic liver disease or carcinoid heart disease.
- Echocardiography is important in clinical/biochemical syndrome to examine tricuspid and pulmonary valves, right-heart dilation and RV function; severe right-sided valve disease changes fluid and vasopressor tolerance.
- Check relevant liver tests, renal/electrolyte losses, nutritional status, planned bowel or liver resection, anticoagulation and availability of vasoactive medication.
- Continue somatostatin analogue prescribed for symptom/tumour control; do not equate being on long-acting therapy with protection against perioperative crisis.
- Discuss crisis criteria and rescue actions at the team brief.

**Intraoperative:**

- Arterial line and good venous access for substantial disease, maintenance of adequate depth, temperature, ventilation and haemodynamic reserve.
- During tumour manipulation, abrupt hypotension or sometimes hypertension/bronchospasm can be a crisis—but first exclude haemorrhage, anaphylaxis, pulmonary embolus, myocardial dysfunction and excessive anaesthetic.
- Ask the surgeon to pause handling, treat major hypotension promptly with titrated noradrenaline/phenylephrine/vasopressin, and consider IV short-acting octreotide as an adjunct if necessary.
- Severe RV failure from carcinoid valvulopathy may need inotropic support as well.
- The October 2026 international consensus says routine IV octreotide prophylaxis is not necessary and does not recommend it as the first treatment of crisis; it does not prohibit discretionary preoperative use for symptom control [R8].
- Use goal-directed fluids for non-hepatic resection; if a liver-resection phase occurs, limit venous congestion while preserving systemic perfusion.

**Postoperative:**

- Consider HDU/ICU after significant clinical/biochemical syndrome, crisis, RV dysfunction, major resection or haemodynamic instability.
- Watch for recurrent instability, bronchospasm, fluid loss, ileus, bleeding and endocrine/nutritional consequences; restart established oncological therapy in consultation with the specialist team.
- Multimodal analgesia and antiemetics help avoid sympathetic and respiratory triggers; historical absolute bans on all catecholamines or morphine are not supported by the current consensus.

items.title: 7. Thyroid disease and thyroidectomy
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 7.1 Hyperthyroidism and hypothyroidism are different physiological threats

- **Hyperthyroidism** raises metabolic rate, tissue oxygen use, HR/contractility and adrenergic sensitivity, while reducing systemic vascular resistance; persistent excess may cause AF, high-output HF, pulmonary hypertension, osteoporosis and loss of muscle mass.
- Thyrotoxicosis does not always produce the classic tremor/goitre: elderly people may present with weight loss, AF or cardiac failure.
- Ask weight loss, heat intolerance, palpitations, diarrhoea, medication (carbimazole/PTU, beta-blockade), adherence, iodine exposure and recent infection.
- Interpret **TSH, free T4 and T3** in context: suppressed TSH + elevated free hormone suggests overt disease; a suppressed TSH with normal free values suggests subclinical disease, but assays/illness/medications complicate interpretation.
- In Graves disease, assess orbitopathy, airway and cardiac complications.
- A large goitre may create tracheal compression/deviation, positional stridor, retrosternal extension and difficult airway risk; CT or nasendoscopy when clinically indicated. [R9]

- **Severe hypothyroidism** reduces CO/HR, impairs ventilatory drive, increases sensitivity to sedatives, can cause hypothermia, anaemia, hyponatraemia and myopathy, and occasionally pericardial effusion.
- Myxoedema coma is a critical emergency with hypoventilation, hypothermia, altered consciousness and shock needing ICU, thyroid hormone (usually IV in severe illness), supportive care and empiric stress steroid coverage while adrenal insufficiency is excluded.
- Mild or treated hypothyroidism rarely warrants cancellation; severe untreated symptomatic disease generally requires optimisation before elective surgery.

## 7.2 Urgent thyroidectomy in uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis

- In principle achieve euthyroidism first through **antithyroid medication** (thionamide), **beta blockade** for rate, and iodine preparation once thionamide is given when appropriate; steroids can reduce peripheral T4→T3 conversion and treat relative adrenal dysfunction in severe thyrotoxicosis.
- In urgent refractory disease, specialist teams may use cholestyramine, plasma exchange or other strategies.
- Assess current hormone values, tachyarrhythmia, LV function, pulmonary pressure, respiratory symptoms, nutrition and airway.
- Do not delay life-saving surgery indefinitely when medical therapy fails, but operate with high-intensity monitoring and a prepared thyroid-storm pathway. [R9]

- Induction: secure airway plan for goitre or tracheomalacia; arterial monitoring for severe instability, careful beta-adrenergic rate control and prevention of pain, hypercarbia, hypoxaemia and sympathetic stimulation.
- Avoid provoking tachycardia and large BP swings; monitor temperature and glucose.
- Ask surgeon to identify recurrent laryngeal nerves and parathyroids; end-of-case check for haemostasis and extubation airway safety.
- Postoperative complications: **neck haematoma/airway obstruction** (immediate airway/surgical emergency—do not delay decompression for imaging), bilateral recurrent laryngeal palsy, laryngospasm, hypocalcaemia/hypoparathyroidism and persistent hyperthyroid crisis. [R9]

## 7.3 Thyroid storm: recognise clinically, treat in parallel

- Storm is life-threatening decompensated hyperthyroidism: hyperthermia, marked tachycardia/AF, CNS disturbance, heart failure/shock and GI/hepatic dysfunction.
- Biochemical hormone concentration alone does not prove storm; clinical severity drives urgent treatment.
- Stop surgery if possible, call for help, oxygen/ventilate, active cooling, careful balanced haemodynamic support and treat precipitants.
- Use **beta-blockade cautiously**, preferably short titratable esmolol in monitored patients if LV function/BP allow; unselected large beta-blocker doses can cause cardiovascular collapse in thyrotoxic cardiomyopathy.
- Start a thionamide, then iodine **after** thionamide where indicated to avoid increased hormone synthesis; hydrocortisone and supportive therapies follow expert protocol.
- Manage arrhythmia, hyperthermia, fluid/electrolyte and hepatic complications in ICU.
- Antipyretic acetaminophen may be used; avoid aspirin, which can displace bound thyroid hormone.
- Never give a single list of drugs without attending to unstable circulatory physiology.

## 7.4 Thyroidectomy and postoperative airway problems

**Beyond thyroid function, surgery itself creates distinctive hazards:**

- Large retrosternal goitre, stridor, tracheal deviation/compression, invasive cancer, prior neck surgery and vocal-cord palsy change the airway plan.
- Evaluate positional dyspnoea, imaging when compressive symptoms exist, and preoperative flexible nasendoscopy where vocal-cord function is uncertain.
- Awake tracheal intubation may be appropriate if induction could lead to loss of an airway that cannot be rescued easily; tracheomalacia after removal of a longstanding compressing goitre is uncommon but possible.
- Plan tube position/neuromonitoring equipment and avoid persistent paralysis if recurrent-laryngeal-nerve EMG monitoring is required.
- Hypervascular Graves disease increases bleeding risk; uncontrolled thyrotoxicosis favours specialist optimisation before elective surgery.

**Airway and metabolic crises after operation:**

- Expanding neck haematoma can cause rapidly progressive obstruction even before external swelling is impressive.
- Recognise distress, stridor, neck tightness, voice change or agitation; summon surgeon/senior anaesthetist immediately and follow the local post-thyroidectomy haematoma protocol, including prompt wound opening/decompression when clinically required rather than waiting for theatre transfer.
- Bilateral recurrent laryngeal nerve injury can cause stridor despite a normal-looking wound; unilateral injury gives hoarseness and aspiration risk.
- Hypoparathyroidism/hypocalcaemia causes perioral tingling, tetany, prolonged QT and rarely laryngospasm/arrhythmia; monitor calcium and treat symptomatic hypocalcaemia promptly.
- Thyroid storm remains a clinical diagnosis; prevent triggers and have beta blockade (if haemodynamically suitable), antithyroid treatment, iodine after thionamide, corticosteroids and ICU support available.
- Postoperative hypothyroidism/thyroid hormone replacement is a longer-term issue rather than an immediate emergence crisis in most patients.

items.title: 8. Calcium, porphyria, pseudocholinesterase deficiency and rarer endocrine problems
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 8.1 Calcium disorders

- **Hypercalcaemia** (primary hyperparathyroidism, malignancy, medicines) causes dehydration/polyuria, constipation, weakness, altered consciousness, nephrolithiasis and arrhythmias (typically shortened QT).
- Severe hypercalcaemia can cause AKI and hypovolaemia, with altered response to neuromuscular blockers and anaesthetic agents.
- Confirm **ionised calcium** or corrected total calcium in context, assess ECG, renal function, volume, phosphate, magnesium and cause.
- Treat severe symptomatic elevations with appropriately cautious isotonic fluid resuscitation, antiresorptive therapy (bisphosphonate or denosumab in suitable malignancy contexts), calcitonin for rapid temporary effect when indicated, and dialysis in selected refractory or renal-failure cases.
- Avoid forced diuresis without overload.
- Parathyroidectomy can lead to rapid postoperative hypocalcaemia and hungry bone syndrome, requiring calcium/magnesium and sometimes active vitamin D replacement.

- **Hypocalcaemia** (parathyroid injury, CKD/vitamin D deficiency, massive transfusion citrate, pancreatitis) causes perioral paraesthesia, tetany, seizures, laryngospasm, impaired contractility and QT prolongation.
- Correct **ionised calcium** and magnesium; if seizure, arrhythmia, severe symptoms or profound low ionised calcium, give monitored IV calcium and repeat measures.
- Transfusion-related hypocalcaemia can worsen hypotension/coagulopathy; replace based on measured ionised calcium and ECG rather than one universal bolus.
- Interpret magnesium and phosphate to prevent recurrence.
- Airway spasm after thyroid surgery is not automatically oedema—consider acute hypocalcaemia and nerve injury.

## 8.2 Acute porphyrias

- Acute hepatic porphyrias (especially acute intermittent porphyria) arise from haem-biosynthesis disturbances; induction of hepatic ALAS1, fasting, stress, infection and unsafe drugs can precipitate accumulation of neurotoxic porphyrin precursors.
- Presentations include severe diffuse abdominal pain without convincing peritonism, autonomic tachycardia/hypertension, hyponatraemia, psychological changes, seizures, weakness and progressive motor neuropathy/respiratory failure.
- A **random urine porphobilinogen (PBG)** during symptoms is an important diagnostic test, interpreted with specialist laboratory advice.
- Check personal/family history of attacks and all prescribed drugs against an up-to-date specialist **porphyria drug-safety database:** blanket ‘all anaesthetic drugs unsafe’ teaching is misleading, and safety classifications are agent-specific.
- Avoid prolonged starvation with glucose-containing nutrition as appropriate; treat precipitant, pain and electrolyte disorders; severe acute attacks may require IV haemin and specialist care.
- In urgent surgery, select verified safe agents, prevent catabolic fasting and observe for respiratory/bulbar weakness and autonomic crises.

## 8.3 Butyrylcholinesterase (pseudocholinesterase) deficiency

- Butyrylcholinesterase metabolises **suxamethonium and mivacurium**, not rocuronium.
- Inherited variants or acquired reductions (pregnancy, liver disease, malnutrition, burns or some drugs) cause prolonged paralysis/apnoea after susceptible NMBA.
- Suspect when postoperative patient remains apnoeic despite appropriate hypnotic recovery; exclude residual nondepolarising block, inadequate ventilation, neurological/metabolic causes and anaesthetic drug accumulation.
- **Do not attempt to reverse suxamethonium block with neostigmine**; sedate, oxygenate and mechanically ventilate until spontaneous neuromuscular recovery, with quantitative monitoring and reassurance.
- Refer for plasma cholinesterase activity/dibucaine number testing and family counselling as appropriate.
- A low dibucaine number indicates atypical genetic enzyme activity; absolute activity also varies with acquired causes.
- Future anaesthesia should avoid suxamethonium/mivacurium, use alternatives (e.g. rocuronium with appropriate reversal) and prominently document the history.

## 8.4 Rapid syndrome discrimination and specific anaesthetic precautions

**Hypercalcaemia:**

- Consider primary hyperparathyroidism or malignancy, with thirst/polyuria, dehydration, constipation, muscle weakness, reduced consciousness, shortened QT and arrhythmias.
- Assess severity, ionised or corrected calcium, ECG, renal function and volume status.
- Treat significant symptomatic hypercalcaemia with monitored rehydration according to cardiac/renal reserve, early cause-specific endocrine/oncology treatment and consideration of calcitonin/antiresorptive therapy; avoid treating ECG changes with an assumed isolated potassium problem.
- **Hypocalcaemia:** causes paraesthesia, tetany, prolonged QT, seizures and potentially laryngospasm; check magnesium and phosphate and treat severe symptomatic cases with carefully monitored IV calcium while addressing the cause.
- Massive transfusion and thyroid/parathyroid surgery are perioperative contexts.

**Acute hepatic porphyria:**

- Neurovisceral attacks may present with severe abdominal pain, autonomic tachycardia/hypertension, neuropathy, hyponatraemia and psychiatric features despite a relatively benign abdominal examination.
- Triggers include prolonged fasting, infection, alcohol and porphyrinogenic drugs.
- Document the exact subtype and drug safety through a specialist medicines database rather than inheriting an inaccurate lifelong 'avoid all anaesthetic drugs' list.
- Provide glucose-containing nutrition when needed, minimise fasting, correct sodium carefully, treat seizures with suitable agents and seek haematology/metabolic input for disease-specific treatment (e.g. haem arginate where indicated).
- A dangerous missed diagnosis is severe motor neuropathy with respiratory weakness.

**Butyrylcholinesterase deficiency:**

- Inherited variants or acquired low activity (liver disease, pregnancy, malnutrition, organophosphate exposure) can prolong succinylcholine or mivacurium paralysis.
- The key rescue is ongoing intubation, ventilation and sedation until spontaneous recovery—an awake paralysed patient is a major preventable harm.
- Quantitative neuromuscular monitoring distinguishes ongoing block from other delayed emergence problems, and investigations include plasma activity and dibucaine number with documentation and family advice.
- Sugammadex reverses suitable aminosteroid block but not succinylcholine-associated phase-I block; no routine antidote exists.
- Use a different neuromuscular blocker next time and make the anaesthetic record explicit.

items.title: 9. Autoimmune, frailty, nutrition and post-transplant comorbidity
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 9.1 Rheumatoid arthritis

- RA can involve **atlanto-axial and subaxial cervical spine instability**, limited TMJ movement, cricoarytenoid arthritis causing dysphonia/stridor, restrictive/interstitial lung disease, pleuritis, pericarditis, myocarditis, vasculitis, renal involvement and chronic anaemia.
- Steroids/DMARDs/biologics increase infection and wound considerations; JAK inhibitors can raise VTE concerns.
- Ask about neck pain/neurology, flexion-related symptoms, voice change, exertional dyspnoea, prior airway difficulty, steroid therapy, infections and functional capacity.
- Examine mouth opening, cervical ROM carefully without provocative forced flexion, neurological status and cardiopulmonary disease.
- Image cervical spine **when symptoms/risk and operation make it clinically useful**, rather than treating a plain film as universally mandatory or a normal neutral view as absolute reassurance.

- For severe cervical instability or limited TMJ, plan **minimal neck movement and first-pass airway safety**, potentially awake fibreoptic technique or video-assisted approach after individualized assessment.
- Cricoarytenoid inflammation may require smaller ETT, gentle instrumentation and postoperative airway vigilance.
- Protect fragile joints/skin and neuropathic limbs during positioning (including prone spinal surgery), avoid extreme neck movement and consider peripheral nerve compression from elbow/knee deformity.
- Steroid stress coverage is individualised.
- Neuromuscular disease and pulmonary fibrosis influence opioid/ventilation strategy.
- Coordinate medication continuation or temporary holding with rheumatology/surgeon according to infection risk and drug, not blanket cessation of all DMARDs.

## 9.2 Systemic sclerosis (scleroderma)

- Scleroderma causes **microvascular dysfunction and fibrosis**.
- Critical perioperative manifestations include microstomia and poor facial mask seal, limited oral opening/cervical mobility, **severe reflux with oesophageal dysmotility and aspiration**, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary arterial hypertension/RV failure, myocardial fibrosis/arrhythmia, renal crisis (rapid hypertension/AKI), Raynaud phenomenon and difficult peripheral vascular access.
- Ask about swallowing/regurgitation, digital ulcers, dyspnoea, functional capacity, prior renal crisis, immunosuppression, current ACEi and evidence of pulmonary HTN.
- Review echo/PFT/CT and renal BP trends when indicated; assess mask/intubation feasibility without assuming low Mallampati predicts easy airway.
- Severe oesophageal stasis can be present despite fasting.

- Prepare for difficult airway and aspiration together: an awake intubation strategy may be safer if both anticipated difficulties are marked, but requires careful planning of regurgitant material and adequate topicalisation.
- Maintain oxygenation, avoid pulmonary vasoconstriction and abrupt falls in systemic BP with PAH/RV disease.
- Preserve warmth and peripheral perfusion for Raynaud’s disease; use temperature monitoring and careful arterial/cuff placement.
- Protect the skin/contractures.
- Monitor BP and kidney function for **scleroderma renal crisis**, which requires urgent specialist treatment (often ACE inhibition) rather than simple management as a volume deficit.
- Pharmacological decisions must respect renal function, cardiac reserve and immunosuppression.

## 9.3 Ankylosing spondylitis

- Ankylosing spondylitis can cause a **fixed kyphotic rigid spine** with fragile ankylosed segments, limited neck extension, temporomandibular movement restrictions, restrictive chest wall mechanics, airway difficulty and aortic root/valve or conduction disease.
- Cervical fractures can occur from minor trauma and may be unstable.
- Plan airway examination, positioning including neutral support and careful transfers, cardiac ECG/echo if indicated and respiratory reserve.
- **Awake fibreoptic intubation** may be a good strategy for severe fixed anatomy, but video techniques may work in selected cases; avoid attempting to straighten a fixed neck.
- Neuraxial anaesthesia can be technically difficult or impossible because of ossified ligaments and altered anatomy; ultrasound may aid assessment, and epidural spread can be unpredictable.
- A spinal/epidural is not automatically safe simply because GA seems difficult—have alternate airway plans.
- Positioning/pressure protection continues throughout long surgery.

## 9.4 Frailty: less reserve than chronological age suggests

- Frailty is multisystem decline in physiological reserve with vulnerability to minor stress; it is not identical to age or disability.
- Evaluate **Clinical Frailty Scale**, baseline ADLs, mobility, falls, cognition, nutrition, weight loss, sarcopenia, sensory deficits, family support and realistic goals.
- Address preoperative anaemia, dehydration without overload, medication burden (anticholinergics, sedatives), delirium risks and likelihood of rehabilitation or loss of independence.
- Risk discussion must include functional outcome, not merely 30-day mortality.
- For urgent major surgery, discuss escalation, ICU and proportionality.
- Intraoperatively avoid prolonged hypotension, deep anaesthesia and large fluid/temperature shifts; dose drugs to physiology, not simply chronological age.
- Postoperatively promote orientation, sleep, pain control without excessive opioids, early mobilisation, hydration/nutrition, hearing aids/glasses and active delirium screening.
- A frail patient can develop pneumonia, AKI, delirium and institutionalisation after a technically successful minor procedure.

## 9.5 Anorexia nervosa

- Anorexia can produce severe **protein-calorie malnutrition, low lean mass, hypoglycaemia, hypotension/bradycardia, QT prolongation/arrhythmia, low cardiac mass, dehydration, hypokalaemic metabolic alkalosis from vomiting, hypomagnesaemia/hypophosphataemia** and impaired immunity/wound healing.
- History should be non-judgmental and include purging/laxatives, intake, recent weight change, psychiatric risk and prior electrolyte instability.
- Check ECG, Mg/PO₄/K/Na/glucose, FBC, cardiac status and aspiration risk.
- Reduce sedative doses in severe malnutrition, avoid hypothermia and monitor volume carefully because atrophic cardiac muscle may not tolerate large boluses.

- A major postoperative danger is **refeeding syndrome:** carbohydrate increases insulin, shifting K/Mg/phosphate intracellularly, risking respiratory muscle failure, heart failure, dysrhythmia and neurological injury.
- Give thiamine and a structured nutrition/electrolyte monitoring plan with dietetics/medical input for high-risk patients.
- Emergency surgery may proceed while severe deficits are corrected concurrently; elective operations should allow stabilisation where possible.
- Respect psychological distress and involve the patient’s treating team.

## 9.6 Anaesthesia after solid-organ transplantation: the patient, graft and drugs

- A post-transplant patient has the physiology of the **transplanted organ**, background disease and ongoing immunosuppression.
- Ask graft type/date, rejection history, last transplant follow-up, current graft function, recent infection, cardiovascular/renal status and exact immunosuppressive regimen/timing.
- **Continue essential maintenance immunosuppression** by agreed oral/IV/NG alternative route unless specialist transplant team instructs otherwise, and protect from missed doses.
- Tacrolimus/ciclosporin cause renal and vascular toxicity, electrolyte changes and have major CYP3A4/P-glycoprotein interactions (e.g. azoles/macrolides and some calcium antagonists); monitor renal function, electrolytes and trough levels as indicated.
- Mycophenolate/azathioprine can impair marrow; steroids may suppress HPA axis; mTOR inhibitors may impair wound healing.
- Infection can present atypically; asepsis, appropriate prophylaxis and early investigation of fever or graft dysfunction matter.

**Previously transplanted heart:**

- Denervation causes resting HR often 90–110, absent normal vagal reflexes and blunted immediate baroreflex chronotropy; responses to atropine may be unreliable, while direct beta agonists, pacing and circulating catecholamines can act.
- The graft is preload-sensitive in some patients, but avoid uncontrolled fluid; assess for **cardiac allograft vasculopathy** (silent ischaemia), rejection, graft systolic/diastolic function and arrhythmia/conduction disease.
- A 2025.1 Final SAQ specifically concerns appendicectomy three years after heart transplant; knowing only that the heart is denervated is insufficient.
- In major illness, high-risk patients need ECG/echo/appropriate cardiac surveillance and transplant liaison.
- The prior Set 13 heart-transplant addendum covers operative graft implantation; **this Set 18 allocation concerns anaesthetising the recipient for non-cardiac surgery**.

**Previously transplanted kidney:**

- Document baseline creatinine, electrolytes, proteinuria/urine, graft age, ureteral anatomy, infections and drug nephrotoxicity; maintain haemodynamic perfusion without volume overload, minimise NSAIDs/contrast and avoid injuring the graft site with access or positioning.
- **Liver transplant:** consider altered metabolism, biliary strictures, renal disease, coagulopathy and immunosuppression; normal LFTs alone do not prove complete long-term reserve.
- Discuss planned surgery, graft concerns, drug interactions and required antibiotic prophylaxis with transplant team.
- Postoperative oliguria, lactate rise, arrhythmia or fever can signal graft pathology and warrants early escalation.

## 9.7 A focused multisystem preoperative decision checklist

**RA versus ankylosing spondylitis versus systemic sclerosis:**

- Rheumatoid arthritis can cause atlantoaxial instability, limited jaw opening and cricoarytenoid disease, plus anaemia, cervical cord symptoms, lung or cardiac disease and drug-related immunosuppression.
- Avoid forced neck movement; seek symptoms and imaging when instability suspected, and use a technique preserving cord safety.
- Ankylosing spondylitis creates rigid fragile spine and fixed kyphosis, difficult positioning/airway and challenging neuraxial access; low-energy fractures may be catastrophic.
- Systemic sclerosis creates a different combination: restricted oral aperture, skin tightening, severe reflux/oesophageal dysmotility with aspiration risk, interstitial lung disease, pulmonary hypertension/RV failure and possible renal crisis.
- An awake intubation can be appropriate in an anatomically difficult airway, but aspiration and poor mouth opening still require a complete rescue plan.
- These conditions are not interchangeable simply because all are 'rheumatological'.

**Frailty and anorexia nervosa:**

- Frailty is a deficit in reserve independent of chronological age.
- Review baseline function, cognition, falls, ADLs, nutrition, mobility, medications, delirium risk, home support and realistic rehabilitation potential; discuss postoperative cognitive and functional outcomes rather than mortality alone.
- Anorexia adds bradycardia, hypotension, QT prolongation, hypokalaemia, hypomagnesaemia, reduced muscle mass and refeeding risk.
- Assess phosphate and glucose when nutrition is restarted; avoid rapid unmonitored carbohydrate or fluid replacement in severe malnutrition.
- Drug volumes of distribution and thermoregulation may be altered.
- Optimise where safe, while recognising that emergency procedures cannot always wait for full nutritional rehabilitation.

**Post-solid-organ transplant:**

- Identify the transplanted organ, time since surgery, rejection/infection episodes, graft function, immunosuppression regimen, prophylaxis and interactions.
- For a heart graft, denervation alters heart-rate responses and makes angina an unreliable marker of allograft vasculopathy; atropine may have little effect, so direct-acting drugs/pacing capability are key.
- For kidney grafts, maintain renal perfusion and monitor calcineurin-inhibitor nephrotoxicity.
- For liver recipients, assess synthetic function and biliary/vascular complications rather than assuming all are permanently coagulopathic.
- In all recipients, avoid missing regular immunosuppression doses and ask whether leucopenia/infection risk changes antibiotic and isolation decisions.
- A transplanted organ does not mean that all non-cardiac surgery requires ICU; risk depends on function, timing and surgery.
- (See integrated Case F.)

items.title: 10. Minor, elective and emergency general/urological/gynaecological surgery
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 10.1 General and endoscopic procedural anaesthesia

- An anaesthetic plan must match **pain, immobility, access, aspiration risk and possibility of rapid escalation**.
- Brief endoscopy can be done under local or monitored sedation in appropriately selected patients; major open surgery usually requires secured airway/controlled ventilation and substantial postoperative analgesia.
- Anaesthesia outside a conventional theatre has the **same monitoring and rescue obligations** as theatre, including oxygen and suction, capnography for sedation where appropriate, readily available airway equipment, an assistant, and a plan to clear obstructions and reach a draped face.
- The failure mode is not merely desaturation but inability to rescue a patient whose sedation unexpectedly becomes GA.

| **Procedure** | **Surgical requirement** | **Anaesthetic decision and principal failure mode** |
|---|---|---|
| Diagnostic laparoscopy / minor elective gynaecology | Short CO₂ pneumoperitoneum, variable lithotomy, uterine manipulation | GA commonly with SGA/ETT according to aspiration/pressure/position; vagal bradycardia with insufflation, shoulder tip pain and PONV; exclude ectopic pregnancy in appropriate patient |
| Minor general surgery/breast biopsy | Supine, local infiltration, variable duration | Local ± titrated sedation, regional or brief GA; avoid overly deep sedation without airway access; plan safe discharge and analgesic requirements |
| Gastroscopy/colonoscopy | Scope shares upper airway; lateral position; possible vomiting/bleeding | Sedation with capnography and airway rescue for stable patient; ETT/GA for active haematemesis, obstruction, significant aspiration risk or complex high-risk ERCP |
| Elective ureteroscopy | Lithotomy, irrigation, endoscope near obstructed upper tract | GA with secure airway often suitable; spinal/selected sedation possible; beware infection, ureteric injury, bleeding, pressurisation and post-op colic |
| Emergency ureteric decompression | Infected blocked kidney, septic shock, urgency | Antibiotics/cultures, resuscitation and urgent drainage (stent or nephrostomy); aspiration and rapid vasopressor needs; avoid delaying source control |
| Emergency diagnostic laparoscopy | Ruptured ectopic, torsion, perforation, obstruction | Pregnancy test, haemorrhage/aspiration/volume assessment, blood access and conversion plan; surgery proceeds with resuscitation |
| Emergency gastroscopy | Haematemesis, obstruction or foreign body | Recognise major aspiration/bleeding risk, coordinate airway control, blood products, prokinetic only when appropriate; anticipate haemodynamic collapse at induction |

**Colonoscopy bowel preparation:**

- Polyethylene glycol–electrolyte lavage is generally isotonic and better tolerated in many patients than sodium phosphate; sodium phosphate can cause large phosphate/calcium/renal disturbances and should be avoided in vulnerable CKD/elderly patients.
- Fasting and catharsis create actual volume deficit; sedatives can cause hypotension.
- Sedation may be monitored propofol using titrated increments with full rescue capability; deep sedation under hypoxaemia risk requires capnography and immediate airway access.
- Procedural complications include perforation, bleeding after polypectomy, aspiration, vasovagal episodes and delayed infection, not only drug-related apnoea.

**Gastroscopy in bleeding/obstruction:**

- Actively bleeding upper GI lesions create aspiration and shock risk; balance the haemodynamic consequences of rapid sequence induction against the consequence of a contaminated airway.
- Large-bore blood access, preoxygenation and haemostatic resuscitation are essential, and the GI/endoscopy team should be ready for immediate intervention.
- Stable screening procedures do not need a routine tracheal tube, while a shocked actively vomiting patient often does.
- ERCP may be prone/semi-prone with access restriction: in severe cholangitis, sepsis, obstructed stomach or prolonged therapeutic procedure, a cuffed ETT is frequently the safer option.
- Abdominal distension can impair ventilation; pancreatitis, perforation, haemorrhage and cholangitis are major post-ERCP complications.

## 10.2 Elective versus emergency laparotomy and laparoscopy: what changes

**Elective open abdominal surgery:**

- Detailed cardiac/pulmonary/renal and anaemia assessment, bowel preparation/nutrition, VTE plan, blood availability, incision-specific analgesia (thoracic epidural in selected large open procedures, abdominal wall catheters, TAP/rectus sheath, PCA), antimicrobial timing and ERAS.
- Mechanical and inflammatory losses demand **individualised balanced fluid**; neither blind generous nor aggressive restrictive fluid reduces harm.
- Monitor core temperature and urine/electrolytes, use blood conservation and prevent pulmonary complications by effective analgesia and mobilisation.
- Prior Set 17 contains the full emergency laparotomy teaching; Set 18 applies it to pelvic and renal operations.

**Emergency laparotomy:**

- Identify obstructed/perforated/infected bowel, contaminated full stomach, vasoplegia, bleeding and organ injury.
- Stabilise induction with blood/vasopressor as mechanism demands, place an arterial line when it will not delay urgent care, give timely antibiotics and obtain early source control.
- A wound closure plan and ICU bed are part of the anaesthetic plan.
- Non-essential cardiac testing and correction of chronic HbA1c should not delay source control.
- Some patients need abbreviated damage-control surgery/relook rather than prolonged definitive reconstruction.

**Laparoscopy:**

- CO₂ pressure increases SVR via sympathetic/neurohumoral effects, can reduce venous return and renal perfusion at high intra-abdominal pressure, and increases PaCO₂/ETCO₂ through absorption.
- FRC/compliance fall, diaphragm moves cephalad, and steep Trendelenburg further increases venous congestion and airway pressures.
- Mild oliguria during pneumoperitoneum is not automatically hypovolaemia.
- Insufflation can trigger bradycardia/asystole (peritoneal stretch), CO₂ embolism, subcutaneous emphysema, pneumothorax, respiratory acidosis and major vessel injury.
- Communicate pressure (often aim 10–15 mmHg or lower when technically feasible), position, duration and need to release insufflation in a crisis.

## 10.3 Rapid intraoperative crisis differential during laparoscopy

**Bradycardia within seconds of insufflation:**

- Likely vagal reflex; tell surgeon **stop and desufflate**, oxygenate, check ECG/BP/ETCO₂, treat atropine or other resuscitation as indicated, reassess before slow re-insufflation at lower pressure.
- A severe collapse may also be gas embolism or major bleeding.
- **Sudden low ETCO₂ with hypotension:** severe fall in pulmonary blood flow from CO₂ gas embolism/PE, haemorrhage, cardiac collapse or circuit disconnection.
- Stop insufflation, give 100% oxygen and resuscitate; check field, equipment and echo when available.
- **Rising ETCO₂/high airway pressures:** CO₂ load, subcutaneous emphysema, endobronchial intubation (tube moves with head-down position), atelectasis, bronchospasm, pneumothorax and ventilator failure; inspect patient/circuit and modify ventilation/IAP accordingly.
- **Facial/conjunctival oedema:** prolonged head-down plus venous congestion/high crystalloid—plan cautious extubation and postoperative airway observation.

## 10.4 Emergency endoscopy and diagnostic laparoscopy: procedure-specific answers

**Emergency gastroscopy for active upper GI haemorrhage:**

- Assess airway contamination (haematemesis, encephalopathy), circulation (shock, antithrombotics, Hb trend), resuscitation response and likelihood of prolonged therapeutic intervention.
- Resuscitate with IV access, crossmatched blood and appropriate reversal when indicated, give indicated GI-specific treatment with the medical/endoscopy team, and arrange suction and an airway plan before endoscope insertion.
- A cuffed tracheal tube can reduce gross aspiration risk in active massive haematemesis or impaired consciousness, but intubation itself carries major haemodynamic/cardiopulmonary risk and is not routine for all UGIB.
- After intubation protect pressure and coronary perfusion, coordinate endoscopic haemostasis, anticipate rebleeding and transfer to appropriate monitoring.
- If bleeding continues despite endoscopy, plan urgent interventional radiology or surgery; a 'normal' pressure while a high catecholamine infusion runs is not stability.

**Emergency diagnostic laparoscopy for acute abdomen or suspected ectopic pregnancy:**

- Ask whether the patient is actually bleeding or septic rather than choosing a low-risk 'laparoscopy' plan.
