- In a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, pregnancy-related airway and aspiration considerations coexist with concealed haemorrhage; secure adequate IV/blood access, use haemostatic resuscitation and prevent haemodynamic collapse with induction and insufflation.
- Do not rely on estimated visible blood loss or a reassuring early haemoglobin.
- In sepsis/peritonitis, treat antibiotics and source control promptly, use graded induction and vasopressor support for vasoplegia, and consider conversion to laparotomy if access or source control is inadequate.
- For ovarian torsion urgent laparoscopy, expedite surgery while screening severe pain/vomiting and aspiration risk.
- The same laparoscopy-induced fall in preload/CO may be tolerated in a stable outpatient but precipitate collapse in haemorrhagic shock.

**Emergency minor gynaecological procedures:**

- Examination under anaesthesia, evacuation of retained products or uterine instrumentation may involve ongoing uterine haemorrhage, sepsis, pregnancy-related aspiration risk and cervical stimulation.
- Confirm haemodynamic stability, pregnancy status, antibiotics when indicated and blood availability; ask about uterotonics and perforation risk.
- Regional or sedation may suit selected stable cases, but deteriorating physiology demands a controlled resuscitation/airway plan.
- Postoperatively reassess bleeding and infection rather than clearing a patient merely because the procedure was short.

## 10.5 Emergency urological procedures and the septic obstructed kidney

**Infected obstructed upper urinary tract is a time-critical source-control problem:**

- A stone with fever, hypotension, rising lactate/creatinine, altered mentation or anuria requires antibiotics, resuscitation and prompt decompression via ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy—not prolonged definitive stone extraction in a physiologically unstable septic patient.
- Preoperative work includes cultures if obtainable without delaying antibiotics, renal function, electrolytes (especially K), sepsis severity and aspiration risk.
- Obtain early specialist/ICU help when pressor support or organ dysfunction is present.
- Anaesthetic technique depends on stability and position: a shocked septic patient may need a controlled GA/ETT and noradrenaline support even for a brief stent; local/regional or sedation can be appropriate for selected decompressions with preserved airway and circulation.

- **During decompression, hypotension can worsen because pressurised infected urine and bacteraemia are released.** Monitor closely, avoid unnecessary high-pressure irrigation, use small assessed fluid boluses for documented volume deficit with early vasoactive support for vasoplegia, and correct life-threatening hyperkalaemia/acidosis.
- Do not interpret low urine output from unilateral obstruction as identical to global hypovolaemia; evaluate contralateral kidney and bladder drainage.
- Postoperatively observe for sepsis progression, AKI, persistent obstruction, bleeding, stent failure and need for definitive delayed stone management.
- The final exam distinction is **source control now, stone clearance later** in unstable infection.

**Other emergencies:**

- Clot retention/haematuria may require catheter irrigation and cystoscopic evacuation but also evaluation of anticoagulation, major bleeding and bladder perforation
- Testicular torsion requires time-critical exploration, often in a young patient who has eaten and vomited
- Priapism needs pain control, directed examination and urgent urology management.
- A short duration does not imply a small physiological or airway risk.

items.title: 11. Robotic pelvic surgery and prolonged Trendelenburg
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 11.1 Why robotics is different

- Robotic prostatectomy, radical hysterectomy and endometriosis/pelvic malignancy surgery frequently involve steep head-down tilt and CO₂ pneumoperitoneum, sometimes for many hours.
- Once the robot is docked, **airway, IV lines and patient position are difficult to access** [R19].
- Confirm secure tracheal tube, oxygenation/ventilation, lines with extensions, capnography, temperature, eyes, arms and legs, circuit tubing and bleeding-rescue equipment before docking.
- Agree on **emergency undocking** and responsibility for releasing robotic arms; do not wait until a cardiac arrest to work out how to reach the chest.

![Interaction between pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg](set18-fig2.png)

Interaction between pneumoperitoneum and steep Trendelenburg

**Respiratory:**

- Head-down displaces diaphragm, lowers compliance and FRC, increases atelectasis and peak/plateau pressures; CO₂ absorption drives minute-ventilation requirements.
- Use lung-protective tidal volumes based on predicted body weight, individualized PEEP/recruitment and ABG if ETCO₂ underestimates PaCO₂ (obesity, lung disease, long cases).
- If severe hypercarbia/pressure cannot be safely managed, ask for lower IAP or less head-down tilt.
- Do not accept dangerous hypercarbia in pulmonary hypertension/RV dysfunction without review.

**Cardiovascular:**

- Raised IAP may decrease venous return/CO; sympathetic response raises SVR and MAP; Trendelenburg raises venous filling/CVP and may worsen HF without necessarily improving effective CO.
- Do not equate high CVP with fluid responsiveness.
- Venous congestion may worsen renal perfusion and airway swelling.
- **Eye/CNS:** raised venous and intraocular pressure, corneal abrasion, rare optic complications and raised ICP in vulnerable patients.
- **Positioning:** nerve stretch/compression (ulnar, brachial plexus, femoral, obturator, sciatic, peroneal), DVT, rhabdomyolysis and well-leg compartment syndrome during prolonged lithotomy.
- Avoid shoulder-brace traction and extreme hip flexion, protect fibular head/heels, reassess position and keep duration reasonable.

**Emergence:**

- Lower legs and flatten table before judging ventilation; check ETT position, reverse NM block quantitatively, evaluate facial/tongue/conjunctival oedema and consider a cuff leak if indicated (imperfect sensitivity).
- Extubate awake and head-up with a rescue plan; delay extubation if swelling or ventilatory reserve is inadequate.
- In PACU watch stridor, hypoventilation/OSA, eye injury, leg pain (possible compartment syndrome), AKI, VTE and concealed pelvic bleeding.
- Document duration of Trendelenburg/lithotomy and any intraoperative pressure/ventilation difficulties.

## 11.2 A structured robotic case: induction, docking, crisis and extubation

**Preoperative:**

- Define procedure and expected tilt/duration, obesity/OSA or pulmonary hypertension, glaucoma/raised ICP, previous neck pathology, difficult airway, significant heart failure and VTE risk.
- Discuss alternatives if steep Trendelenburg is unsafe.
- Arrange an ETT rather than an unsecured airway for steep, prolonged robotic surgery; secure tube/eyes/lines before inaccessible positioning, choose IV extension lengths, check fixation and padding and ensure the operating team can rapidly undock.
- An arterial line is reasonable for prolonged major procedures or significant comorbidity, but not an automatic requirement for every robotic case.

**After insufflation and docking:**

- Expect increased PaCO₂ and peak airway pressure, reduced compliance/FRC and possible reduction in effective venous return despite raised measured CVP.
- Use predicted-body-weight tidal volumes, titrated PEEP and ventilatory rate, check pressure plateau and trends, and request a lower insufflation pressure or less tilt when necessary.
- Document duration and protective positioning.
- Urine output is less reliable as a surrogate of filling status during high IAP; don't repeatedly bolus fluid to chase mild oliguria.
- For a sudden rise in airway pressure, systematically check ETT depth/kink, atelectasis, bronchospasm, subcutaneous emphysema and pneumothorax.
- For rapid hypotension/low ETCO₂, announce crisis and undock/desufflate, examine for bleeding or gas embolism and resuscitate according to physiology.

**Undocking and recovery:**

- Correct fluid and temperature abnormalities, reverse paralysis with quantitative evidence, restore supine/head-up positioning before interpreting ventilation, and assess for facial, lingual and laryngeal oedema.
- An absent cuff leak is not definitive but can support an airway concern.
- Delay extubation if severe swelling, hypercapnia, residual weakness or inadequate oxygenation persists.
- Following prolonged lithotomy investigate disproportionate calf/thigh pain, tense compartments, weakness or sensory changes urgently; a regional block or analgesics must not delay compartment assessment.
- Watch PONV, hypoventilation/OSA, eye injury, rhabdomyolysis, VTE and occult pelvic bleeding.
- A clear emergency undocking protocol is as important as selecting an induction agent.

items.title: 12. Urological operations: procedure-specific physiology and complications
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 12.1 TURP and endoscopic bladder surgery

- TURP/HoLEP and transurethral bladder tumour resection (TURBT) commonly occur in elderly patients with CAD, CKD, prostate obstruction or infection.
- The scope distends the bladder and resects vascular tissue while irrigation clears blood.
- Monopolar electrocautery historically requires **electrolyte-free hypotonic solutions** (glycine/sorbitol), whereas bipolar resection generally uses **normal saline**.
- Absorption through opened prostatic venous sinuses or perforation can cause acute fluid loading.
- Classic **TUR syndrome** combines dilutional hyponatraemia/hypo-osmolality, neurological symptoms, pulmonary oedema, dysrhythmia and haemodynamic change; glycine may also cause visual disturbance/hyperammonaemia.
- Saline reduces classic hypo-osmolar TUR syndrome but **can still cause hypervolaemia and hyperchloraemic acidosis**.
- Longer resection, high bag pressure and capsular perforation increase risk.

- Preoperative assess anticoagulants/antiplatelets, infection/urine culture, renal function, Na/K, Hb and cardiopulmonary reserve.
- **Spinal anaesthesia** can allow early detection of nausea, confusion and visual changes and avoids airway instrumentation; GA is equally valid when indicated and requires vigilance for haemodynamic/lab clues.
- If neuraxial, screen antithrombotic timing and avoid overly high block.
- During resection, discuss irrigation medium and return-volume monitoring, time and bag pressure; monitor BP/ECG, mental state if awake, temperature and low threshold for ABG/sodium with instability.
- Beware occult blood loss diluted by irrigant; maintain group-and-screen/crossmatch when expected bleeding significant.
- For lateral-wall bladder tumours, obturator nerve stimulation can cause sudden adductor jerk and bladder perforation unless adequate NM block or selective obturator block is used.

**Suspected fluid absorption/TUR syndrome:**

- Stop irrigation/resection, ABCDE, oxygen/ventilate, quantify deficit, sodium/osmolality/ABG/ECG, examine pulmonary congestion and distinguish acute water overload from major haemorrhage.
- For **severe symptomatic acute hyponatraemia** (seizure, coma, profound confusion), controlled 3% hypertonic saline boluses under local hyponatraemia protocol aim for an **initial 4–6 mmol/L rise**, then avoid overcorrection; manage acute pulmonary oedema with oxygen/PEEP and diuresis when truly hypervolaemic, with ICU/electrolyte monitoring.
- Do not use 3% saline simply because a mild low sodium is discovered in an otherwise well patient.
- Postoperatively assess bleeding/clot retention, bladder perforation, sepsis, TUR syndrome and catheter discomfort.

## 12.2 Ureteroscopy, ureteric stenting, lithotripsy and PCNL

- **Ureteroscopy** accesses ureter/renal collecting system; guidewires, dilation, stones and laser fragmentation require immobility and reliable irrigation return.
- Obstruction plus infection is **urological sepsis** requiring rapid cultures, antibiotics and drainage (ureteric stent or percutaneous nephrostomy); stone removal may be deferred until infection controlled.
- Irrigation under high pressure can cause pyelovenous/pyelolymphatic reflux, bacteraemia, perinephric fluid extravasation and AKI.
- Preoperative assess renal function, sepsis, urine culture/antibiotic, bleeding and previous stents.
- An upper-tract procedure may provoke vagal response, arrhythmia, pain and postoperative renal colic.
- GA with ETT or SGA is commonly feasible according to airway/position and pressure; spinal is possible in selected cases.
- If severe septic shock, choose a stable induction with prepared vasopressors, assess actual fluid responsiveness and involve ICU early.

**Extracorporeal shock-wave lithotripsy (ESWL):**

- Targeting/immobility, repeated shock waves and analgesia/sedation, with potential haematuria, perirenal haematoma, arrhythmia (sometimes ECG-gated shocks), renal colic, obstruction by stone fragments and infection.
- Position varies; assess pregnancy status (usually contraindication), anticoagulants/coagulopathy, pacemaker/ICD and procedural device policies, renal infection and lesion location.
- Anaesthesia may be titrated sedation, regional or GA depending on equipment, pain, cooperation and duration.
- Plan airway access with positioning and communicate shocks/ECG gating.

**Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL):**

- Large stone burden, percutaneous kidney tract, often prone, with higher bleeding and collecting-system perforation risks, possible adjacent pleural/lung injury (especially upper-pole access), haemothorax/pneumothorax, sepsis and significant irrigation absorption.
- A high-risk patient with staghorn calculus needs cultures, antibiotics, blood availability, renal assessment and safe prone positioning/secure tube and lines.
- Maintain perfusion, check temperature and bleeding, use postoperative pneumothorax/sepsis surveillance.
- Specific flank/retroperitoneal analgesia and catheter/stent discomfort require a multimodal plan.

## 12.3 Major urological cancer surgery: nephrectomy, cystectomy, prostatectomy

**Partial nephrectomy:**

- Preserve renal parenchyma while obtaining vascular control; hilar clamping produces warm ischaemia, and unclamp/reperfusion can cause bleeding or renal injury.
- CTA/renal function and contralateral reserve guide risk.
- Preoperative ask CKD, hypertension, cardiac disease, solitary kidney, antithrombotics, tumour extent and suspected vena caval thrombus.
- Intraop coordinate clamp start/end and expected duration, blood availability and renal perfusion pressure; do not advocate unproven routine mannitol/diuretic renal protection.
- After surgery monitor Hb, renal function, urine, bleeding, urine leak and infection.
- **Radical nephrectomy** may require lateral position and possible renal vein/IVC work; large venous tumour thrombus can demand advanced monitoring, echo, massive transfusion and cardiothoracic/vascular backup.

**Radical cystectomy/urinary diversion:**

- Lengthy pelvic dissection with variable major blood loss, bowel resection for ileal conduit or continent diversion, high fluid and electrolyte shifts, infection and venous thrombosis risk.
- Preoperative treat anaemia, malnutrition, renal dysfunction, smoking and infection; confirm neoadjuvant chemo toxicity and need for bowel segment.
- Intraoperative monitor haemostasis/temperature and fluid response, consider epidural or abdominal wall catheters for open procedure, avoid excessive crystalloid that worsens bowel oedema while preserving renal perfusion.
- Postoperative ileus, anastomotic/urinary leak, metabolic **hyperchloraemic acidosis** with urinary bowel diversions, AKI, sepsis, VTE and stoma viability are key.
- Early mobilisation, nutrition and tailored analgesia matter.

**Open prostatectomy:**

- Major pelvic venous bleeding potential and need for good postoperative analgesia; consider epidural or regional truncal blocks, haemorrhage planning and catheter concerns.
- **Robotic prostatectomy** usually has less incisional pain/blood loss but adds steep head-down/CO₂ physiology and restricted access; postoperative airway swelling/nerve injury are important.
- Ask whether a patient is taking androgen deprivation, anticoagulants or has obstructive uropathy, and whether a pelvic lymphadenectomy is planned.
- Maintain perfusion, consider restrictive-to-euvolemic individualised fluid strategy, do not use aggressive controlled hypotension at the expense of kidneys/eyes/optic perfusion.
- Check catheter/bleeding postoperatively; urinary anastomotic leak and VTE require surveillance.

## 12.4 Urological decision points: prevention and rescue

**TURP/TURBT fluid syndrome:**

- Ask at briefing whether irrigant is electrolyte-free/hypotonic (monopolar) or isotonic saline (bipolar/HoLEP), anticipated duration and potential capsular/bladder breach.
- Under spinal, new headache, nausea, confusion, visual disturbance or bradycardia may reveal rapid glycine/sorbitol absorption; under GA, unexplained hypoxaemia, hypotension/hypertension, rhythm change or reduced sodium may be the clue.
- Stop resection, inform urologist, evaluate fluid balance and obtain ABG/electrolytes/osmolality.
- Manage airway and pulmonary oedema, carefully restrict additional fluid, assess loop diuretics if overloaded and obtain critical-care support.
- Severe symptomatic hypotonic hyponatraemia with seizures or profound neurological change may require controlled 3% saline boluses under a formal local hyponatraemia protocol; avoid both delayed treatment and overrapid sodium correction.
- Saline irrigant can still cause volume overload or hyperchloraemic acidosis without hyponatraemia.
- TURBT introduces additional obturator nerve stimulation from lateral-wall diathermy, causing adductor jerk and potential bladder perforation; deep neuromuscular blockade or obturator nerve block may be required with the surgical plan.

**PCNL and stone surgery:**

- Prone positioning reduces airway access and can compromise venous return, particularly with abdominal compression; ensure ETT/eye/pressure protection before turning.
- Large renal vessels may bleed invisibly, with transfusion or embolisation required.
- Thoracic pleural injury, pneumothorax, hydrothorax, infection and fluid absorption are relevant; obtain postoperative chest evaluation if symptoms or a supracostal tract raise suspicion.
- Lithotripsy (ESWL) creates movement/analgesia needs, sometimes cardiac rhythm-related gating and risk of haematoma or obstruction; distinguish it from invasive ureteroscopy and PCNL.
- Ureteroscopy complications include ureteric injury/perforation, sepsis, fluid overload and postoperative stent pain.

**Major cancer resection:**

- Open radical cystectomy includes bowel diversion, significant tissue injury, blood loss, long operative duration, fluid/temperature shifts, bowel ileus, renal impairment and high VTE risk.
- Robotic prostatectomy involves long steep Trendelenburg/CO₂ and secure airway; postoperative bleeding/urinary anastomosis/obstruction requires surveillance even after minimal skin incision.
- Radical/partial nephrectomy can cause major vascular bleeding (renal vein or caval involvement), loss of renal function and potential adrenal injury.
- For a mass with IVC thrombus, define cephalad extent with imaging and plan vascular/cardiothoracic support, large-bore access, rapid transfusion and potentially advanced monitoring.
- Partial nephrectomy may use renal hilar clamping; protect contralateral renal function and address postoperative bleeding/urinary leak.
- Analgesia choices change with incision, renal function and anticoagulation; a large epidural is not automatically suitable for a robotic incision or for a patient expected to receive anticoagulants.

items.title: 13. Gynaecological surgery, hysteroscopy and fertility treatment
items.priority: P1 CORE (2 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (3 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 13.1 Gynaecological disease features that alter anaesthesia

**Heavy uterine bleeding/fibroids:**

- Evaluate chronic iron-deficiency anaemia, ongoing haemorrhage, fibroid size/mass effect, prior abdominal surgery and potential rapid blood loss at hysterectomy/myomectomy.
- **Endometriosis:** chronic pelvic pain, opioid tolerance, adhesions and difficult dissection (bowel/ureter/bladder) increase pain and conversion risk; severe deep infiltrating disease may require extended pelvic surgery with bowel/ureteric involvement.
- **Pelvic malignancy:** anaemia, weight loss, ascites, pleural effusion, hypercoagulability, ureteric obstruction/renal impairment, bowel obstruction, chemotherapy toxicity and psychosocial stress.
- **Ectopic pregnancy or torsion:** emergency bleeding or time-critical organ preservation; pregnancy possibility and haemodynamic stability must be established in a reproductive-age patient with pelvic pain.
- **Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS)** after fertility treatment can cause capillary leak, ascites, haemoconcentration, VTE and reduced perfusion.

- Preoperative pregnancy test where clinically appropriate, discuss fertility and consent, review hormonal therapy/anticoagulation, chronic pain/analgesics and previous postoperative PONV, evaluate pelvic mass respiratory/venous effects and obtain appropriate blood products.
- Avoid assuming laparoscopy is low risk merely because the incision is small: large ovarian masses, deep endometriosis and malignant pelvic dissection can be complex and prolonged.

## 13.2 Hysteroscopy: fluid deficit is a safety variable, not a theatre accounting detail

- Diagnostic hysteroscopy and operative myomectomy/polypectomy use a distended uterine cavity.
- Complications include **uterine perforation** (bleeding, visceral injury), haemorrhage, cervical trauma, infection, air/gas embolism (rare) and systemic absorption of distension medium through exposed venous sinuses.
- The medium matters: monopolar systems may use electrolyte-free hypotonic glycine/sorbitol (hyponatraemia, cerebral oedema, visual disturbance/hyperammonaemia), while modern bipolar/mechanical systems commonly use **saline** (avoids dilutional hyponatraemia, but absorption can still cause volume overload and pulmonary oedema).

- Before starting, know whether the operation is diagnostic versus deep myometrial resection, anticipated duration, pressure, medium and **agreed maximum deficit**.
- The BSGE/ESGE guidance uses upper stopping limits in otherwise healthy women of **1000 mL hypotonic** or **2500 mL isotonic** medium; **lower limits** approximately 750/1500 mL are advised for elderly or cardiac/renal patients.
- These are upper safety thresholds, not a mandate to continue in a symptomatic patient until the number is reached; stop much earlier if rapid absorption or neurological/respiratory signs occur.
- Record and announce cumulative deficit throughout surgery and at handover. [R10]

![Hysteroscopy distension-fluid decision and escalation](set18-fig3.png)

Hysteroscopy distension-fluid decision and escalation

- Technique may be local cervix block ± sedation for limited diagnostic work or GA/spinal for prolonged operative resections; choose according to pain, uterine manipulation, airway and aspiration risk.
- Under sedation, nausea/headache/confusion may signal irrigant absorption rather than an antiemetic deficit.
- Under GA, look for unexplained hypertension then bradycardia, hypoxaemia, pulmonary oedema or reduced cerebral function on emergence; blood gas/electrolytes are essential.
- If fluid overload suspected: stop procedure/medium, ABCDE, check sodium/osmolality, volume and ECG, support oxygenation/ventilation, treat acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with controlled hypertonic saline and overload with appropriate diuresis, seek ICU help.
- If perforation suspected with instability or rising abdominal distension, alert surgeon and assess for abdominal injury/bleeding, potentially laparoscopy/laparotomy.

## 13.3 Infertility: oocyte retrieval and endoscopic treatment

- Transvaginal ultrasound-guided oocyte retrieval is usually short but painful during follicle puncture and often requires deep sedation or GA with careful airway and haemodynamic monitoring; lithotomy allows procedural access, and needle passage risks vaginal/pelvic bleeding, infection and organ injury.
- Ovarian response and recent hormonal therapy can cause **OHSS** with distension, ascites, dyspnoea, hypovolaemia despite total-body fluid excess, thrombosis and renal dysfunction.
- Check symptoms and stage before elective retrieval; severe OHSS may require admission/critical care rather than routine ambulatory discharge.
- Analgesia can use carefully titrated propofol/opioid, paracervical block or other techniques; coordinate clinic-specific practices, pregnancy-related considerations and recovery escort.
- Other fertility surgery may include diagnostic laparoscopy or operative hysteroscopy, with the respective CO₂ and distension-fluid hazards.

## 13.4 Gynaecological cancer surgery and radical pelvic procedures

**Radical hysterectomy ± lymphadenectomy:**

- Longer surgery, potential ureter/bladder or bowel injury, pelvic venous bleeding, lymphatic leakage, lithotomy/Trendelenburg neuropathies and postoperative VTE.
- **Ovarian cancer cytoreduction:** may involve major laparotomy, diaphragmatic stripping, bowel resection, splenectomy, extensive blood loss, large inflammatory losses, ascites and uncertain ability to achieve complete resection; postoperative ventilation/ICU often required in high-risk patients.
- Prior chemotherapy can cause thrombocytopenia/anaemia, renal toxicity, peripheral neuropathy and cardiac dysfunction.
- **Pelvic exenteration:** extremely long high-blood-loss operation with bowel and urinary diversion and multiple anastomoses; anaesthetic concerns span large-bore blood access, temperature, haemostatic therapy, fluid/vascular perfusion, prolonged positioning, renal compromise, antibiotic planning, intensive analgesia and postoperative ICU.

- Before major surgery, assess nutrition/anaemia, VTE, reno-ureteric obstruction, bowel symptoms, cardiorespiratory reserve and oncological goals.
- Consider neuraxial analgesia for open laparotomy where antithrombotic/bleeding circumstances permit, plus truncal blocks, acetaminophen and opioid rescue.
- During surgery, avoid both hypotension/AKI and indiscriminate fluid overload that worsens bowel oedema, wound/anastomotic healing and respiratory function; use assessed boluses, vasopressor for vasodilation and blood products for haemorrhage.
- After surgery anticipate ileus, occult haemorrhage, urinary leak/AKI, bowel anastomotic leak, infection, thromboembolism, lymphatic leak, neuropathic pain and the needs of new stomas and rehabilitation.

## 13.5 Surgical emergencies in gynaecology and infertility care

**Gynaecological procedures differ by physiological burden:**

- Elective diagnostic laparoscopy/ovarian cystectomy generally needs short-acting GA, PONV prophylaxis and limited opioid exposure; severe endometriosis surgery may involve rectovaginal/bowel or ureteric dissection and prolonged pneumoperitoneum, raising bleeding, visceral injury and postoperative pain risks.
- Open hysterectomy or cytoreduction may require blood products, active warming, renal and coagulation monitoring, multimodal/neuraxial or truncal analgesia and HDU planning.
- Radical pelvic cancer operations can include bowel resection, ureteric reconstruction or exenteration; understand the planned sequence and potential major vessel involvement rather than describing all as 'hysterectomy'.
- In 2026 ERAS Society guidance for gynaecological oncology, goal-directed fluid management and multimodal analgesia are emphasized for major surgery; use this along with individualized surgical requirements rather than one fluid quota [R21].

**Hysteroscopy is a pressure/absorption problem as well as an anaesthetic:**

- Before starting, confirm monopolar vs bipolar system, hypotonic vs isotonic solution, expected duration, uterine-perforation risk and fluid deficit method.
- Have the circulating team call out deficit trends; the deficit is not equal to intravasation if there are leaks/spillage, but is the safety metric.
- The BSGE/ESGE guideline's upper stopping deficits for a healthy patient are 1,000 mL hypotonic and 2,500 mL isotonic, reduced to approximately 750/1,500 mL for significant cardiac/renal comorbidity [R10].
- Actual clinical symptoms warrant action earlier.
- Acute neurological deterioration with hypotonic fluid should prompt emergency sodium/osmolality testing; normal sodium does not exclude isotonic volume-overload pulmonary oedema.
- Consider perforation, haemorrhage and embolism in unexpected collapse.

**Fertility treatment:**

- Transvaginal oocyte retrieval is commonly short IV anaesthesia/deep sedation with analgesia and immediate airway rescue; be alert to aspiration risk, procedural bleeding, vagal response and rare infection.
- Ovarian hyperstimulation syndrome (OHSS) is a separate high-risk presentation: enlarged ovaries, capillary leak, ascites/pleural effusions, haemoconcentration, AKI and thromboembolic risk.
- Assess respiratory compromise, intravascular volume and coagulation, correct severe derangement and coordinate reproductive/critical care teams rather than treating it as ordinary postoperative nausea.
- A large, enlarged ovary is vulnerable to torsion; do not overlook acute abdomen or pregnancy-related causes of pain after fertility treatment.

items.title: 14. Breast surgery and regional analgesia

items.body:
- Breast-conserving surgery may need only GA, paravertebral block or local infiltration, whereas mastectomy with axillary clearance/reconstruction involves more pain, shoulder limitation and lymphatic/vascular considerations.

Sensory innervation:

- **T2–T6 intercostal anterior and lateral cutaneous branches** cover much of the breast.
- The **intercostobrachial nerve (T2)** supplies upper medial arm/axilla.
- Supraclavicular nerves (C3–4) contribute superior breast/clavicular skin.
- Pectoral nerves innervate pectoralis muscles (not the whole skin field).

- Innervation varies and dense complete surgical anaesthesia may require multiple targets.

**Analgesic options and trade-offs:**

- Surgical infiltration, PECS I (between pectoralis major/minor for pectoral nerves), PECS II (additional plane between pectoralis minor/serratus anterior for lateral thoracic/intercostal territory), serratus anterior plane, thoracic paravertebral block (unilateral multilevel segmental coverage), or erector spinae plane as a potentially more superficial approach.
- For mastectomy with axillary work, **PECS II or paravertebral** is often a reasonable choice; the former may inadequately cover parasternal skin and the latter has pleural, hypotension and deep-block anticoagulant implications.
- Adjust for tumour site, axillary incision, bilateral surgery, antithrombotic therapy and total local anaesthetic dose across surgeon infiltration and blocks.
- A successful block reduces opioids but does not guarantee prevention of chronic postsurgical pain. [R11]

- Position arm abduction carefully after axillary surgery and protect nerves; check cardiac toxicity of prior anthracyclines/trastuzumab and lung effects of radiotherapy.
- Flap reconstruction may need a long operation, microsurgical perfusion and a **goal-directed normovolaemic/vasopressor** plan rather than indiscriminate fluid loading.
- Postoperatively watch haematoma, flap perfusion, PONV, pain, upper limb function, infection and chronic neuropathic symptoms.
- After discharge provide wound, analgesic and physiotherapy instructions appropriate to procedure.

## 14.1 Breast anaesthesia: distinguish operation and block coverage

**Operations:**

- Lumpectomy, mastectomy, sentinel node sampling, axillary clearance and immediate reconstruction differ substantially in cutaneous territory, pectoral manipulation, drain requirements, duration and expected postoperative pain.
- Assess cancer therapy effects (chemotherapy-related cardiotoxicity, radiation fibrosis/respiratory limitation, lymphoedema), existing neuropathic pain, PONV susceptibility and anxiety; discuss arm positioning and pressure protection.
- Day-case breast conservation often suits GA with local infiltration plus multimodal analgesia; mastectomy/axillary clearance merits a regional technique and a stronger rescue plan.
- Autologous reconstruction has its own prolonged surgery, blood-flow and postoperative flap surveillance needs, covered mainly in Set 17/Plastics.

**Block reasoning:**

- Thoracic paravertebral block covers ipsilateral thoracic somatic nerves with more reliable deep unilateral segmental spread, but carries neuraxial/pleural/haemodynamic risks; PECS I addresses medial/lateral pectoral nerves and PECS II adds lateral upper thoracic/intercostal and often intercostobrachial territory, useful for axilla, yet medial parasternal incision may be incompletely covered.
- Serratus anterior plane block is useful for lateral chest wall/axillary distribution but not universally for medial breast; erector spinae spread is variable and may not match the entire surgical field.
- Local infiltration and superficial cervical plexus/parasternal supplementation may be required.
- No one block replaces surgeon-provided infiltration, systemic analgesia or rescue; include local-anaesthetic systemic-toxicity and anticoagulant considerations.

**Postoperative:**

- Actively prevent PONV, monitor respiratory effects of opioid and regional technique, examine for haematoma and problematic axillary pain, provide clear oral transition and discharge advice.
- Persistent postmastectomy pain can be neuropathic (intercostobrachial nerve injury), so early identification and referral for persistent symptoms matter, while no one regional block has definitive prevention evidence.

items.title: 15. Renal transplantation: a high-priority complex operation
items.priority: P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs) + P3 MODERATE (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 15.1 Surgical sequence determines the physiological goals

- Renal transplantation generally places a donor kidney **extraperitoneally in an iliac fossa**, with vascular anastomoses to external iliac (or alternative iliac) vessels followed by graft reperfusion, ureteroneocystostomy/stenting and closure.
- The recipient’s native kidneys usually remain in situ.
- **Deceased donor** transplantation is relatively time-critical and may involve prolonged cold ischaemia, whereas a **living donor** procedure allows more planned timing and potentially shorter ischaemia.
- Surgical concerns include iliac vessel calcification, prior transplants, adhesions, thrombosis/atheroma, graft size, haemorrhage, urinary leakage and early graft thrombosis.
- For a detailed account of implantation read BJA Education [R18] alongside newer BEST-Fluids evidence; before starting, confirm precise anastomotic site, clamp/reperfusion timing, expected cold/warm ischaemia, unusual donor features and the immunosuppression regimen.

![Renal transplantation: assessment, reperfusion and early complications](set18-fig4.png)

Renal transplantation: assessment, reperfusion and early complications

## 15.2 Preoperative assessment: dialysis status is not a substitute for fitness

- Ask cause and duration of ESRD, dialysis type/last session, **dry weight, residual urine production**, intradialytic hypotension and heparin, AV fistula site, infection/access status, prior transplant or sensitisation, transfusions, pregnancy, diabetes and drug regimens.
- Check: potassium, bicarbonate, sodium, Hb/platelets, calcium/phosphate/Mg, ECG, creatinine/urea, liver status, coagulation, glucose and HbA1c.
- Investigate CAD/HF/valve disease/PAH with history, function and targeted echo/stress evaluation; some ESRD patients have severe silent CAD, LVH, diastolic dysfunction or vascular calcification.
- Bone/mineral disorder, uraemic platelet dysfunction, immune vulnerability and chronic anaemia increase risk.
- Dysautonomia and gastroparesis may influence aspiration and induction.
- Review dialysis within roughly 24 hours when possible, but **do not over-dialyse to profound underfilling**; confirm K/volume immediately preoperatively.
- An AV fistula arm should be protected from cuff and unnecessary cannulation. [R12,R13]

**Medication questions:**

- What immunosuppression induction and maintenance will be given (basiliximab, antithymocyte globulin, methylprednisolone, tacrolimus/ciclosporin, mycophenolate)?
- When are each due?
- What reactions, marrow suppression or haemodynamic changes can occur with an infusion?
- Is there antiviral/antibiotic prophylaxis?
- Review insulin, antihypertensives, anticoagulants and drugs with renal clearance or neurotoxicity.
- Discuss incision analgesia and renal safety before surgery.
- A plan based only on creatinine and potassium misses cardiac risk, infection, access and transplant-specific perfusion requirements.

## 15.3 Intraoperative technique and monitoring

- GA with secured airway is usual; consider aspiration risk from diabetes/uraemia and standard fasting status.
- Use invasive arterial pressure where significant haemodynamic risk, unreliable cuff readings or complex transplant justify it; reliable IV access and blood availability matter.
- Avoid ipsilateral dialysis fistula cannulation and damaging compromised veins.
- A central line is not mandatory in all cases but can be justified for inadequate access or complex vasoactive infusions.
- Doppler/echo or dynamic cardiac-output monitoring may help complex cardiac/volume decisions, but neither CVP nor urine output alone proves fluid responsiveness.
- Keep warm, monitor ABG/K/Ca/glucose, consider renal-safe NM blocker selection and use opioid/sedative doses appropriate to renal clearance (morphine active metabolites may accumulate; remifentanil/fentanyl often easier intraoperatively). [R12,R13]

**Before reperfusion:**

- The main goal is adequate graft blood flow at an appropriate systemic perfusion pressure without making a cardiac patient fluid overloaded.
- Reassess blood loss, haemoglobin, temperature, potassium/acidosis and actual volume responsiveness; ensure surgeon announces release.
- Titrated balanced crystalloid and noradrenaline for vasodilation may be more physiological than repeated unnecessary fluid boluses.
- Some transplant teams target MAP in the 80–90 mmHg range around reperfusion, but an absolute universal target is unsupported; account for chronic hypertension, LVH/CO and local protocol.
- High doses of pure vasoconstrictor can reduce organ flow if cardiac output falls; monitor perfusion, not a pretty MAP.
- **Avoid routine ‘renal-dose’ dopamine** and avoid relying on mannitol/furosemide as proven prevention of delayed graft function. [R12,R13,T2]

**Fluid type matters:**

- BEST-Fluids, an Australasian multicentre RCT in deceased-donor kidney transplantation, showed that **low-chloride balanced crystalloid reduced delayed graft function compared with 0.9% saline** [T2].
- High chloride may promote renal vasoconstriction and hyperchloraemic acidosis; the small potassium content of balanced crystalloid is not proof it causes clinically important hyperkalaemia.
- Use balanced crystalloid as a default unless another specific indication, with repeated glucose/K/acid-base measurement.
- Avoid hydroxyethyl starch in AKI-prone recipients.
- The goal is assessed euvolaemia and graft perfusion, **not CVP 12 or a predetermined litre count**.

## 15.4 At reperfusion: a perfusion problem, not a diuretic challenge

- When clamps open, graft appearance, Doppler flow, systemic BP and sometimes immediate urine are reassuring, but **early urine is not a definitive test of graft viability**, especially with ischaemic deceased-donor grafts.
- If hypotension occurs, assess blood loss/venous pooling/vasodilation, dysrhythmia, anaphylaxis or myocardial function; correct based on mechanism.
- Check K/acidosis if instability or prolonged ischaemia, adjust perfusion and inform surgeon.
- If no urine appears, examine renal blood flow and potential anastomotic problem rather than reflex escalating furosemide and flooding a failing LV.
- Delayed graft function may require dialysis while the graft recovers; the possibility must be explained preoperatively and included in postoperative monitoring.

**Analgesia:**

- Multimodal paracetamol, limited opioid adjusted to renal function, local infiltration, TAP/QL/ESP blocks in suitable cases.
- Thoracic epidural/neuraxial or intrathecal opioid may be used selectively but evaluate uraemic platelet dysfunction, residual dialysis heparin and postoperative anticoagulants/need for early neurological review.
- Avoid routine NSAIDs because early graft perfusion is vulnerable.
- A continuous truncal block can provide incision analgesia without sympathectomy, but calculate total local anaesthetic exposure and consider the patient’s size, plasma proteins and systemic disease.

## 15.5 Postoperative renal transplant care

**Immediate priorities (PACU/ICU):**

- Airway/oxygenation and pain
- BP, HR, effective perfusion and fluid status
- Serial hourly urine output in context of baseline residual urine, graft type and reperfusion
- Potassium, acid–base, glucose and creatinine
- Drain/haematoma/bleeding and graft Doppler if poor perfusion.
- Avoid hypotension and volume depletion but do not chase polyuria with litre-for-litre crystalloid if it produces congestion; conversely, marked posttransplant diuresis can cause true volume loss and electrolyte derangements.
- Coordinate a fluid balance plan with transplant nephrology, including expected losses and triggers for additional assessment.

- **Early complications to identify by mechanism:**

| **Problem** | **Clinical clues** | **Response** |
|---|---|---|
| Graft vascular thrombosis/stenosis | Abrupt oliguria/anuria, pain/swelling, impaired Doppler or rising creatinine | **Immediate transplant/vascular review and Doppler**; revascularisation may be time-critical |
| Ureteric obstruction/kink or urinary leak | Low urine, wound/drain urine, graft swelling, hydronephrosis | Ultrasound/imaging, assess stent and surgical anastomosis; early operative/urological consultation |
| Delayed graft function / acute tubular injury | Inadequate filtration especially deceased donor; K/acidosis/volume changes | Exclude obstruction and arterial/venous catastrophe; renal support/dialysis if standard indications, avoid nephrotoxins |
| Haemorrhage/haematoma | Tachycardia, Hb decline, pain, hypotension, graft compression | Urgent assessment, blood support, ultrasound/CT or return to theatre as needed |
| Hyperkalaemia and metabolic changes | Weakness, ECG toxicity, acidosis, reduced output | Immediate ECG/calcium for toxic hyperK, shifting/elimination strategy, reassess graft/dialysis indications |
| Acute rejection/infection | Creatinine rise, altered graft function, fever may be absent under immunosuppression | Early transplant review, cultures/viral investigation or biopsy as indicated; do not empirically withdraw all immunosuppression |
| Cardiovascular/respiratory deterioration | Pulmonary oedema, myocardial injury, AF, sepsis | Assess volume, echo, ECG/troponin when warranted, oxygenation and sepsis source |

**Immunosuppression management:**

- Accurate administration time/dose and trough levels matter; tacrolimus/ciclosporin interact with azoles, macrolides and other CYP inhibitors and can cause nephrotoxicity/hyperkalaemia.
- Mycophenolate and antithymocyte therapy may suppress leukocytes and predispose to infection.
- Surgical infection prophylaxis, asepsis and viral prophylaxis are transplant-team dependent.
- Keep lines/catheters only as long as required, encourage early nutrition/mobilisation and plan patient education for rejection and infection red flags.
- A patient with **postoperative oliguria plus hypotension** needs both haemodynamic assessment and urgent exclusion of graft vascular/ureteric cause; do not label it ‘contrast nephropathy’ by default. [R12,R13]

## 15.6 Postoperative transplant problems: time, cause and treatment

**First 0–24 hours:**

- Document cold/warm ischaemia context, donor type, preoperative residual urine and any intraoperative vascular/anastomotic problem.
- Monitor hourly output and serial creatinine, potassium, bicarbonate, glucose and haemodynamics, with clinical/ultrasound assessment of volume and cardiac congestion.
- Early oliguria/anuria requires urgent evaluation of effective perfusion, haemorrhage, acute vascular thrombosis or kinking, renal vein thrombosis, obstruction at ureteric anastomosis or catheter, and ischaemia–reperfusion injury/ATN.
- Confirm catheter patency and seek graft Doppler/ultrasound promptly when indicated.
- A functioning kidney can produce high early urine output and salt wasting; replace real intravascular losses thoughtfully with transplant input, avoiding blind litre-for-litre targets that cause pulmonary oedema in LVH/HF patients.

**Delayed graft function:**

- Commonly defined in trials as dialysis required within the first postoperative week; this definition is operational and may reflect clinical dialysis thresholds.
- It is more common after deceased-donor grafts and ischaemic injury.
- Distinguish from acute rejection, technical vascular complication, obstruction, hyperacute immunological injury and calcineurin-inhibitor toxicity; Doppler and potentially biopsy depend on timing and trajectory.
- Dialysis is not a transplant failure diagnosis and may be needed for refractory hyperkalaemia, acidosis, volume overload or uraemic complications while recovery occurs.
- BEST-Fluids supports balanced low-chloride crystalloids in deceased-donor renal transplantation [T2], not a fixed high-volume protocol.

**Days to weeks:**

- Surveillance includes wound/urinary infection, sepsis masked by immunosuppression, lymphocele, ureteric leak/stricture, thromboembolism, hyperglycaemia, electrolyte wasting, tacrolimus/ciclosporin troughs and interaction/renal toxicity.
- Rejection can present with deteriorating function rather than pain/fever.
- Do not miss prescribed induction/maintenance immunosuppressants or prophylaxis, and coordinate medication administration with graft/nephrology pharmacy.
- For a worsening creatinine, assess haemodynamics, Doppler, obstruction, infection, nephrotoxins and immune causes together.
- A concise oral SAQ answer should follow: perfusion → surgical graft patency → renal/metabolic support → immunosuppression/infection → long-term graft surveillance.

items.title: 16. Practical perioperative analgesia, fluids and fast-track recovery
items.priority: P1 CORE (1 parent LO) + P2 HIGH (2 parent LOs)
items.body:
## 16.1 Analgesia must match the incision, patient and follow-up

**Minor/endoscopic procedures:**

- Local infiltration/paracervical or penile block when appropriate, paracetamol and short-acting opioid rescue; avoid prescribing several days of strong opioids for an uncomplicated 20-minute hysteroscopy or screening colonoscopy.
- **Laparoscopy/robotics:** multimodal analgesia, local port infiltration ± TAP/QL/ESP as appropriate, paracetamol and selected NSAID if renal/bleeding risk permits, opioid rescue; prophylaxis for PONV and CO₂ shoulder pain.
- **Major open pelvic/abdominal surgery:** thoracic epidural can be valuable for dynamic pain and pulmonary mechanics but may cause sympathectomy/hypotension and is constrained by antithrombotics
- Abdominal wall catheters, bilateral TAP/rectus sheath or QL blocks treat somatic incisional pain but do not fully treat visceral pain
- Combine with PCA as needed.
- **Renal transplant:** favour renal-safe choices, avoid routine NSAID and assess uraemic bleeding before deep or neuraxial block.
- **Breast/axilla:** PECS II or paravertebral with explicit field limitations.
- **Chronic pelvic pain and opioid-tolerant patients:** continue established baseline opioids safely, address neuropathic features, psychological distress and avoid unplanned withdrawal, with discharge coordination.

- A genuinely useful analgesic plan names: the expected pain generator (somatic incision, visceral dissection, bladder spasm, ureteric colic), technique and coverage, breakthrough treatment, side effects, anticoagulant restrictions, monitoring, plan for block failure, and handover/discharge transition.
- A large regional block doesn’t absolve clinicians from neurological checks (e.g. compartment syndrome after lithotomy) or systemic opioid monitoring.

## 16.2 Perioperative fluids by operation and time point

- **Always distinguish maintenance, replacement and resuscitation**.
- In an elective short endoscopy, large empiric IV volumes are unnecessary.
- During major abdominal or pelvic surgery, sustained low MAP/CO threatens kidneys, bowel anastomoses and flaps, while excessive crystalloid causes lung/airway/wound and bowel oedema.
- Treat haemorrhage primarily with blood and haemostatic components when indicated, vasodilatory hypotension with targeted vasoactive support, and genuine preload responsiveness with assessed balanced-crystalloid boluses; check response and fluid tolerance.
- Dynamic PPV/SVV is invalid or unreliable in spontaneous breathing, arrhythmia, low tidal volume, high IAP or right-heart dysfunction.
- Urine output during pneumoperitoneum can fall from elevated pressure even when the patient is euvolaemic. [T3]

| **Situation** | **Primary circulatory issue** | **Why treatment differs** |
|---|---|---|
| **Phaeo before vein ligation** | Catecholamine-mediated hypertensive surges and variable LV function | Smooth depth, short titratable vasodilator and rate control; avoid unnecessary preload/indirect agents |
| **Phaeo after ligation** | Abrupt loss of catecholamines, vasoplegia, possible low output | Stop vasodilator, direct vasopressor ± assessed volume, echo for myocardial dysfunction |
| **Carcinoid crisis** | Mediator-related severe vasodilation ± RV disease | Vasopressor first line, octreotide adjunct, assess bleeding/anaesthetic alternatives |
| **Robotic pelvic surgery** | High IAP, raised venous pressures, impaired lung mechanics | Avoid both hypoperfusion and oedema; CVP misleading; preserve eye/airway safety |
| **Open pelvic cancer** | Blood loss, bowel manipulation, capillary leak | Blood-based replacement for haemorrhage; tested crystalloid; prevent sustained AKI-causing hypotension |
| **Renal graft reperfusion** | Graft needs perfusion without LV overload | Balanced low-chloride crystalloid, assessed CO/preload and BP; exclude thrombosis if no graft function |
| **Diabetes with SGLT2 exposure** | Hypovolaemia, ketosis possible without marked hyperglycaemia | Glucose, ketones, ABG and K; insulin+dextrose pathway for ketoacidosis |
| **Sepsis from obstructed kidney** | Vasoplegia and source-control need | Antibiotics/urinary drainage, assessed fluid and early noradrenaline when indicated |

- The Australasian RELIEF trial found no disability-free survival advantage of a strongly restrictive regimen and **more AKI** with restrictive fluids (8.6% vs 5.0%) in higher-risk major abdominal operations [T3].
- This does not endorse indiscriminate liberal infusion.
- The best exam statement is avoid both clinically important under-resuscitation and fluid overload using a monitored, physiology-guided approach.

## 16.3 Enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) in pelvic/urological/gynaecological care

- ERAS integrates **preoperative counselling and nutritional/anaemia preparation, minimised fasting, appropriate carbohydrate strategy (not automatic in poorly controlled diabetes), opioid-sparing analgesia, normothermia, PONV prophylaxis, goal-directed fluid and pressure management, early oral intake/mobilisation and removal of unnecessary lines/catheters**.
- For major cystectomy and oncological pelvic surgery, additional issues are stoma training, bowel-function recovery, VTE prophylaxis, psychological support and renal electrolyte surveillance.
- Do not misinterpret ERAS as ‘no opioids’, ‘no fluids’ or immediate discharge regardless of reserve; it is a coordinated pathway to improve recovery while identifying patients whose infection, ileus, AKI or bleeding makes pathway deviation necessary. [T3,R14]

- Postoperative pain, nausea and urinary retention can delay discharge from simple procedures, but rapid discharge is unsafe when a patient has significant anaesthetic complication, large hysteroscopy fluid deficit, refractory OSA hypoventilation, surgical bleeding or postoperative hypotension.
- For high-risk major surgery, a clearly documented HDU/ICU plan and early detection of complications are part of recovery quality.

## 16.4 Worked prescriptions by procedure and stage of recovery

**Minor hysteroscopy or outpatient ureteroscopy:**

- Analgesia typically begins with paracetamol, selected NSAID if kidney/bleeding risk permits, local infiltration/paracervical techniques and a short-acting opioid rescue only if needed.
- Expect bladder spasm/ureteric stent discomfort rather than major incisional pain; counsel on haematuria, urinary retention and sepsis red flags.
- A same-day patient with refractory pain, tachycardia, hypotension, fever or unexpected bleeding requires evaluation, not simply another opioid prescription.

**Robotic prostatectomy/hysterectomy:**

- Port-site infiltration ± TAP/QL block for somatic pain, paracetamol, judicious NSAID if safe, PONV prophylaxis and limited rescue opioid.
- Major pressure/ventilatory and VTE risks may exceed incision pain.
- Fluid strategy should avoid congestion/facial oedema during steep Trendelenburg while preserving organ perfusion; use vasopressor for documented anaesthetic vasodilation rather than reflex fluid loading, replace true bleeding with appropriate blood/components and reassess after desufflation.
- If the patient has OSA, favour monitored opioid-sparing recovery and early CPAP where appropriate.

**Open cystectomy/major pelvic cancer surgery:**

- Preoperative anaemia/nutrition/renal assessment, consent for blood products, VTE strategy and coordination of epidural/anticoagulants.
- Intraoperatively use patient-specific balanced fluid, invasive haemodynamic monitoring when indicated, active warming and blood conservation.
- An epidural can provide dynamic analgesia for a large incision but hypotension, mobilisation difficulties and catheter anticoagulant timing matter; TAP/rectus sheath/QL or wound catheters with PCA provide alternatives, especially with expected therapeutic anticoagulation or neuraxial contraindications.
- Postoperatively anticipate ileus, stoma/urinary diversion electrolyte loss, urinary leak, infection, AKI and prolonged VTE risk; oral intake, mobilisation and discharge medication transition are key ERAS endpoints, not optional extras.

**Major gynaecological laparotomy:**

- Manage laparotomy versus extensive peritoneal stripping/HIPEC or bowel resection as different burdens.
- Analgesia often includes epidural or truncal catheter plus acetaminophen/selected anti-inflammatory drugs and opioid PCA; adapt to bowel anastomosis, renal function, coagulopathy and VTE prophylaxis.
- Use early recognition of haemorrhage, abdominal compartment physiology, ileus or sepsis to guide fluids, vasopressor and ICU escalation.
- The 2026 gynaecologic oncology ERAS guidance supports goal-directed fluid therapy and multimodal analgesia; it does not mean keeping a patient under-resuscitated to meet a fixed restriction target [R21].

**Anticipating failed fast-track recovery:**

- Failure to mobilise may reflect anaemia, orthostasis, uncontrolled movement pain, delirium or neuromuscular/nerve injury.
- PONV or ileus may reflect excessive opioids, bowel handling, electrolyte derangement or an anastomotic leak; investigate persistent deterioration.
- Multimodal treatment should name the pain source, dose/route and monitoring, options if epidural or block fails, antiemetic and thromboprophylaxis timing, discharge analgesic duration and a safety-net for re-presentation.

items.title: 17. Oncological emergencies and treatment complications
items.priority: P5 MINIMUM (1 parent LO)
items.body:
## 17.1 Superior vena cava obstruction (SVCO)

- Thoracic cancer or thrombosis may obstruct venous return from head, neck and upper limbs causing facial/arm swelling, plethora, distended neck veins, dyspnoea, cough and sometimes **stridor, cerebral oedema, headache, confusion or syncope**.
- Risk depends on speed and collateral development: gradual obstruction may be tolerated, acute thrombosis or associated mediastinal mass less so.
- CT/venous imaging defines obstruction; tissue diagnosis should be arranged if stable.
- Severe airway compromise/cerebral oedema is urgent: position head-up, oxygen, avoid unnecessary supine sedation/GA, involve oncology/IR for stenting and treat thrombosis if appropriate.
- In associated anterior mediastinal mass, airway and cardiovascular collapse on induction/positive-pressure ventilation is an additional threat; multidisciplinary awake/local strategy or ECMO-ready centre may be required in very-high-risk cases.
- Prefer lower-limb IV access if SVC return is severely impaired; an upper-limb bolus may be delayed reaching heart. [R15]

## 17.2 Malignant spinal cord compression

- New severe focal back pain (often nocturnal), radicular pain, progressive weakness, sensory deficit, gait difficulty or sphincter symptoms in a patient with cancer is **cord compression until excluded**.
- Perform/document baseline neurological exam, urgent MRI of whole spine according to pathway, immobilisation/pressure precautions when unstable, **dexamethasone per local oncology/spinal protocol** if neurological compromise and urgent surgical/oncology review for decompression or radiotherapy.
- Time to intervention determines irreversible deficits.
- Do not dismiss new weakness after surgery as residual block without evaluation.
- Anaesthesia for decompression must account for spine instability, prone positioning, blood loss and neurological monitoring; postoperative repeat motor assessments are essential.

## 17.3 Malignant pericardial effusion and tamponade

- Tumour infiltration or treatment may produce pericardial fluid.
- Slowly developing large effusion may be initially tolerated; rapid accumulation causes **tamponade**.
- Features: tachycardia, hypotension, raised JVP, pulsus paradoxus (not always present), dyspnoea, oliguria and low output.
- Echo may show RA systolic/RV diastolic collapse, plethoric IVC and marked respiratory variation; interpretation depends on ventilation/pressure and regional loculation.
- **Unstable tamponade requires urgent drainage**, guided by echo and relevant specialist service.
- Before definitive drainage preserve sympathetic tone, avoid severe vasodilation and minimise positive-pressure effects; induction can precipitate collapse.
- A fluid bolus may briefly support an underfilled patient but is not definitive therapy.
- After drainage watch acute haemodynamic shifts, ventricular dysfunction and recurrence.

## 17.4 Treatment-related immunocompromise and graft-versus-host disease (GVHD)

- Cytotoxic chemotherapy, corticosteroids, biologic therapy, haematopoietic cell transplantation and stem-cell–transplant GVHD create risks of **neutropenic sepsis, fungal/opportunistic infection, thrombocytopenia/anaemia, mucositis, hepatic/renal disease, lung injury and malnutrition**.
- Acute GVHD particularly affects skin, GI tract and liver after allogeneic haematopoietic transplantation; diarrhoea can cause severe volume/electrolyte loss and haemorrhage.
- Chronic GVHD can cause pulmonary fibrosis/bronchiolitis obliterans, mucosal and skin fibrosis and difficult airway/ventilation.
- Identify actual immunosuppressants, recent neutrophils/platelets, sepsis, prophylactic drugs and airway changes.
- Use strict asepsis, appropriate source/antibiotic strategy, careful blood product/neuraxial planning and organ-appropriate drug dosing.
- A normal temperature does not exclude sepsis in immunosuppressed patients.
- In critical illness treat infection promptly, support organ failure and coordinate with haematology/transplant service rather than stopping all immunosuppression automatically. [R16]

## 17.5 Other immediate consequences to recognise

**Tumour lysis syndrome:**

- After cytotoxic therapy or in rapidly proliferative haematological malignancy, hyperkalaemia, hyperphosphataemia, hypocalcaemia, hyperuricaemia and AKI cause fatal arrhythmia/seizure risk.
- Check ECG/electrolytes/urate/renal function, institute early fluids when tolerated, urate-lowering therapy (rasburicase or allopurinol according to risk) and urgent renal support if needed.
- **Neutropenic sepsis:** broad-spectrum antibiotics promptly after cultures if feasible without delay, source control and early organ support.
- **Hypercalcaemia of malignancy:** dehydration, arrhythmias and neurological impairment; manage as in Chapter 8. **Bleeding/obstructive tumours:** correct reversible physiology while obtaining definitive haemostatic, vascular or decompressive treatment.
- The LO asks for initial recognition and management, not complete oncological chemotherapy protocols.

items.title: 18. Integrated exam cases: show reasoning rather than listing drugs
items.priority: P1 CORE (4 parent LOs) + P2 HIGH (3 parent LOs)
items.los: BT_PO 1.5; IT_PO 1.4; SS_GG 1.8; SS_GG 1.6; SS_GG 1.1; SS_GG 1.9; SS_GG 1.7
items.body:
## Case A — 63-year-old with type 2 diabetes on dapagliflozin for urgent lower-limb bypass

**Preoperative formulation:**

- This is a vascular patient with systemic atherosclerosis, potentially poor cardiac reserve, renal impairment and a critical-ischaemic limb, and an SGLT2 inhibitor that can precipitate ketoacidosis.
- Find last dapagliflozin/insulin/metformin doses, amount of fasting and whether there is active infection/critical limb sepsis.
- Check ECG, Hb, renal function/K, glucose, **blood β-hydroxybutyrate and bicarbonate/pH/anion gap**, volume/perfusion and antithrombotic therapy.
- Urgency of limb salvage may prevent a three-day drug hold; stopping now does not guarantee immediate absence of risk.
- Explain the risk to surgeon and plan enhanced perioperative ketone monitoring, while treating any actual ketoacidosis before or concurrently with life-saving revascularisation.

**Intraoperative:**

- Choose GA versus regional based on heparinisation, operative extent and cardiopulmonary reserve; invasive arterial monitoring in high-risk disease, maintain tissue oxygen delivery and avoid haemodynamic swings.
- If on type 1 or insulin-deficient treatment ensure continued basal insulin or VRIII with glucose substrate as indicated; stop SGLT2.
- Assess potassium and acid–base during arterial reperfusion.
- If low MAP after clamp release, differentiate vasodilation, bleeding, reduced output and reperfusion toxicity.
- A glucose of 8 mmol/L after surgery does **not** exclude euglycaemic DKA if pH 7.23 and ketones high.

**Postoperative:**

- Hourly/serial blood glucose and appropriate ketone/ABG surveillance while fasting or unwell; renal, potassium, urine/limb and myocardial assessment; reintroduce nutrition and own diabetes regimen only when clinically safe.
- An endocrinology plan for restarting dapagliflozin (after full recovery, eating, no ketosis) belongs in the discharge summary.
- This case also tests the earlier Set 14 vascular principles without repeating that chapter.

## Case B — 56-year-old with phaeochromocytoma for laparoscopic adrenalectomy

**Preoperative:**

- Justify biochemical metanephrine confirmation, anatomical imaging, ECG/echo for arrhythmia/LVH/catecholamine cardiomyopathy, renal/glucose/electrolytes and orthostatic volume assessment.
- Treat with alpha blockade and volume re-expansion as tolerated, then beta blockade only if needed after alpha; document actual BP lying/standing and symptoms.
- Discuss day-of-surgery monitoring, vasodilators, blood access, anticipated tumour-manipulation and post-ligation phases with the surgeon.
- A surgeon asking simply ‘what beta-blocker should I start?’ before alpha control deserves a clear contraindication rationale.

**Intraoperative:**

- Arterial line and prepared short titratable vasodilator plus noradrenaline.
- Smooth induction; monitor BP/HR/ECG, haemodynamics and glucose.
- During tumour handling BP 230/110, HR 140: stop manipulation and control catecholamine physiology.
- After vein ligation MAP 48: stop vasodilator, treat vasoplegia with direct vasopressor and evaluate blood loss/volume responsiveness/LV function.
- **Postoperative:** monitor hypo/hypertension, arrhythmia, catecholamine-withdrawal hypoglycaemia, adrenal insufficiency when relevant and renal injury.
- This is the core P1/P2 endocrine operative case.

## Case C — Severe systemic sclerosis with oesophageal dysmotility for laparoscopy

**Preoperative:**

- Identify microstomia/airway difficulty and major aspiration risk, ILD and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) with RV dysfunction, renal crisis history, Raynaud’s vascular access and immunosuppression.
- Obtain symptoms/clinical risk-directed TTE, lung testing and renal/BP assessment; conventional fasting does not exclude retained oesophageal material.
- Discuss awake intubation feasibility if difficult ventilation/intubation coincides with aspiration risk; prepare suction, gentle airway handling and tailored induction.
- The absence of stridor is not proof that the airway is straightforward.

**Intraoperative:**

- Protect systemic BP and RV coronary perfusion; avoid hypoxaemia, hypercapnia, acidosis, high airway pressure and excessive PEEP that increase PVR; low pressure CO₂ pneumoperitoneum and limited Trendelenburg if feasible.
- Keep warm, cushion skin/joints and monitor haemodynamics and urine.
- Titrate fluids and vasoactives by CO/perfusion; do not force a fixed CVP.
- **Postoperative:** check oxygen/respiratory reserve, aspiration, renal BP/creatinine, pain and infection.
- This case demands integrated multisystem prioritisation instead of a rote checklist.

## Case D — Hysteroscopic myomectomy with a rising distension-fluid deficit

- At prebrief the surgeon states bipolar resection with saline, 120-minute possible duration.
- Agree fluid deficit alarm points and lower maximum if renal/HF disease, identify monitoring lead and obtain baseline Na if risk.
- During surgery deficit rapidly rises toward 1.5 L, ventilation pressures increase and patient becomes hypoxaemic.
- **Do not wait for a ‘normal’ sodium:** isotonic saline absorption can cause pulmonary oedema without hyponatraemia.
- Ask for procedure stop and reassessment, review hemodynamics and irrigant accounting, ABG electrolytes and lung ultrasound/CXR, support airway/oxygenation/PEEP and treat true volume overload.
- If instead hypotonic glycine is used and the patient develops confusion, seizure and Na 112, treat as **acute symptomatic hyponatraemia** with monitored 3% saline according to guideline while protecting airway.
- In both scenarios communicate fluid **type**, deficit and net IV fluid; report to recovery team for delayed deterioration. [R10]

## Case E — Kidney transplant from deceased donor in a patient with ESRD and LVH

**Preop:**

- Yesterday’s dialysis, volume/dry weight, K, AV fistula, cardiac reserve/diastolic dysfunction, prior sensitisation, immunosuppression and access.
- **Intraop:** preserve coronary and graft perfusion; select balanced low-chloride crystalloid and check K/ABG/glucose, avoid large fixed boluses in stiff LV, communicate anastomosis and reperfusion.
- Before clamp release MAP 65, CO low and lungs congested: another litre might worsen pulmonary oedema, so assess LV filling and afterload before selecting a vasopressor/inotrope strategy.
- When kidney reperfused but urine absent, investigate graft perfusion and anastomoses, and consider delayed graft function—not automatic large-dose diuretics.
- **Postop:** serial K/creatinine, graft Doppler if concern, urine in context, meticulous drug dosing/troughs, infection prevention and safe analgesia.
- State the BEST-Fluids result and its relevance to crystalloid choice; no need to memorise a universal CVP target.

## Case F — Previously transplanted heart, emergency appendicectomy

**Preop:**

- Three years post-heart transplant, evaluate donor graft function and rejection/allograft vasculopathy (often silent angina), recent follow-up, immunosuppression and CKD/infection.
- Ask why appendicectomy is necessary and whether sepsis/peritonitis is present.
- ECG and focussed echo/investigation as clinically warranted; do not delay urgent source control for routine invasive coronary angiography in a stable patient.
- **Intraop:** anticipate resting higher HR, denervation, altered response to atropine and autonomic reflexes; use appropriate **direct-acting** haemodynamic drugs and correct sepsis or haemorrhage by mechanism, not routine fluid overload.
- Monitor BP/HR, renal, oxygenation and aspiration; continue immunosuppression schedule or arrange alternative route.
- **Postop:** graft perfusion, arrhythmia, renal function, infection and medication levels/interactions, with transplant liaison.
- The core point is not that every recipient needs an arterial line but that allograft status and immunosuppression matter in addition to denervation.

## Case G — Robotic hysterectomy in severe obesity: difficulty ventilating after docking

- Before docking, a 52-year-old with BMI 47 and OSA is positioned in lithotomy/steep Trendelenburg; airway/line access will be restricted.
- Ramped preoxygenation, secure cuffed ETT and quantitative block monitoring; ensure eye/arm/peroneal protection and robot undocking plan.
- During dissection ETCO₂ rises to 58 mmHg and plateau pressure increases; differential includes increased CO₂ absorption, cephalad diaphragm, atelectasis, endobronchial ETT, bronchospasm and pneumothorax/subcutaneous emphysema.
- Inspect circuit and position, verify tube, increase minute ventilation if safe, optimise PEEP/recruitment, ask surgeon to reduce IAP/tilt if needed, and ABG to assess PaCO₂/acid-base when there is substantial physiological uncertainty.
- Near end, marked facial swelling raises risk of airway obstruction: head-up recovery and assessment of ventilation/airway oedema, full reversal, awake extubation with rescue; defer extubation if not safe.
- After surgery resume CPAP and check neurological/leg symptoms.

## Case H — Oncology patient with new paraplegia, superior vena caval obstruction or tamponade

- The question may say ‘a patient with cancer becomes breathless/weak/collapses’.
- First distinguish pathway, not simply increase oxygen.
- Head/neck swelling and positional stridor imply SVCO or mediastinal airway compromise: keep head-up and urgently involve specialists, avoiding destabilising GA if possible.
- New back pain with leg weakness implies **metastatic spinal cord compression:** document neurological examination, MRI and urgent dexamethasone/spinal review.
- Hypotension with effusion and RV collapse suggests **tamponade:** urgent drainage with haemodynamic stability before/through intervention, avoid reflex severe vasodilation/PPV.
- Chemotherapy with sepsis and neutropenia requires rapid antimicrobials/source control rather than awaiting WCC response.
- An examiner expects a distinct initial management plan for each, not one ‘oncology emergency’ list.

items.q: Discuss the perioperative management of an adult patient who underwent heart transplantation three years ago and now requires an appendicectomy.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Assess graft function, altered physiology/drug responses, continue immunosuppression, include appendicectomy physiology and postoperative care; avoid distraction by an assumed pacemaker.

### Assessment and preparation
Treat appendicitis as urgent: assess sepsis, aspiration risk, hydration, electrolytes and renal function while contacting the transplant team. Establish graft function, exercise tolerance, recent echo/ECG, rejection episodes, cardiac allograft vasculopathy (CAV), arrhythmia, tricuspid regurgitation and any actual device. CAV may be silent; absence of angina is insufficient reassurance. New dysfunction or arrhythmia warrants targeted investigation without indiscriminate delay for routine tests.

Confirm all immunosuppressant names, doses and last administration. **Continue immunosuppression on schedule**, arranging an alternative route with the transplant service if nil by mouth; do not simply omit it. Check calcineurin-inhibitor concentrations when indicated, nephrotoxicity, K/Mg, marrow suppression, infection and drug interactions (including macrolides/azoles). Continue usual steroid; assess need for perioperative supplementation from dose, duration and surgical stress. Use asepsis and appropriate appendicitis antibiotics.

### Physiology and drugs
Denervation commonly produces a faster resting rate and attenuated immediate baroreflex responses; cardiac output responds to venous return and circulating catecholamines. Partial reinnervation is variable. Preserve adequate filling **without routine fluid loading**, especially with diastolic dysfunction, sepsis or renal impairment.

Direct catecholamines such as noradrenaline/adrenaline/isoprenaline remain effective and may produce marked responses; titrate. Ephedrine has mixed direct/indirect effects and is less predictable, not invariably ineffective. Atropine/glycopyrrolate chronotropy is unreliable; have direct chronotropy and pacing available. Adenosine sensitivity may be increased. Neostigmine-associated bradycardia has been reported despite denervation; use quantitative neuromuscular monitoring and an appropriate reversal plan.

### Anaesthesia and operation
If laparoscopic, pneumoperitoneum, positive pressure and head-up positioning can reduce venous return, while CO2 absorption and increased afterload add cardiac stress. Agree low insufflation pressure and immediate desufflation for unexplained instability. GA with a secured airway suits an urgent full-stomach patient; titrate induction to sepsis and graft reserve, prepare vasopressors, use ECG/SpO2/capnography/temperature and consider an arterial line if unstable or significantly impaired. Maintain oxygenation, normocapnia, perfusion, temperature and renal protection. Diagnose hypotension by cause rather than relying on reflex tachycardia or repeatedly giving fluid.

### Postoperative care
Choose monitored recovery/HDU/ICU according to graft dysfunction, sepsis and intraoperative events. Provide effective analgesia and ventilation, careful fluid/renal and rhythm review, timely immunosuppression and infection surveillance. Escalate new dysfunction for rejection/CAV assessment; give a named medication and transplant follow-up handover.

items.q: You are asked to assess and anaesthetise a 54-year-old patient for a laparoscopic cholecystectomy. They received a heart transplant ten years ago. Discuss the issues relevant for this patient.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Discuss denervation/drugs, immunosuppression and present graft function; explicitly address pneumoperitoneum.

### Establish current risk ten years after transplantation
Review original disease and transplant course, exercise tolerance, rejection, CAV surveillance, recent graft/valve and RV function, ECG/rhythm and any genuine pacing indication. Late CAV can be clinically silent; a long interval since transplant does not mean normal risk. New dyspnoea, dysfunction or arrhythmia needs transplant/cardiology assessment. Check renal impairment, hypertension, diabetes, infection/malignancy and medicine interactions; obtain targeted ECG, echo and laboratory tests rather than routine invasive investigations.

### Denervation and its practical consequences
Resting HR is often elevated and the immediate reflex response to low preload or vasodilation is blunted. Sympathetic/parasympathetic reinnervation is variable by ten years and cannot be assumed from elapsed time. Preserve venous return without overfilling. Silent ischaemia means haemodynamics, ECG and appropriate biomarkers matter more than angina alone.

Direct vasoactive drugs work: titrate noradrenaline for vasodilation and direct chronotropy/inotropy or pacing if required. Atropine is unreliable. Ephedrine is mixed acting, with variable effect. Adenosine may cause exaggerated block; neostigmine can cause bradycardia. Use quantitative blockade monitoring and a considered reversal plan.

### Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
CO2 insufflation can reduce venous return, increase SVR and cause hypercapnia; reverse Trendelenburg adds preload loss. These effects matter particularly when reflex compensation is impaired. Agree gradual low-pressure insufflation, careful position changes and desufflation if instability persists. Use a titrated GA with controlled ventilation, adequate analgesia and vasopressor availability. Add an arterial line for significant graft dysfunction or haemodynamic risk. Avoid hypoxaemia, major CO2 rise, hypothermia and prolonged hypotension; guide small fluid challenges by actual response.

### Immunosuppression and postoperative plan
Continue immunosuppressants without missed doses and arrange alternative administration if necessary. Check calcineurin nephrotoxicity, electrolytes, concentrations when indicated and antimicrobial interactions. Continue steroid and assess stress supplementation. Use asepsis, appropriate surgical antibiotics and renal-adjusted analgesia; avoid unnecessary nephrotoxins.

Plan monitored recovery and higher care for poor graft reserve or instability. Resume oral drugs on time, document fluid/renal/rhythm surveillance, infection review and responsibility for contacting the transplant service. Any new ventricular dysfunction or arrhythmia requires investigation rather than automatic attribution to anaesthesia.
