items.q: Discuss how Marfan syndrome influences your anaesthetic management for a patient requiring an urgent laparoscopic appendicectomy.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Prioritise cardiovascular BP control during laryngoscopy, pneumoperitoneum and emergence, airway and pulmonary/pneumothorax issues. Avoid exaggerated routine invasive/ICU plans or a generic septic full-stomach recipe.

### Key problem and assessment
Marfan syndrome is a connective-tissue disorder, commonly due to an FBN1 variant, with **aortic-root aneurysm/dissection, AR and mitral prolapse/MR** of greatest immediate cardiovascular concern. Assess usual surveillance imaging, aortic dimensions/growth, prior repair, valve function, symptoms and beta-blocker/ARB therapy. New abrupt chest/back pain, pulse/BP discrepancy, syncope or AR raises acute dissection: obtain urgent specialist imaging and change priorities. A current normal symptom history alone does not exclude aortic disease.

Urgent appendicitis adds sepsis, dehydration and aspiration risk. Review anticoagulation if prior mechanical valve and any pregnancy possibility. Obtain ECG and targeted echo/CT only for a management-changing question without unnecessary delay.

### Other systems that change anaesthesia
Look for difficult airway features (high-arched palate, crowded teeth, joint/cervical instability), chest deformity, scoliosis/restrictive physiology, bullae or prior spontaneous pneumothorax. Assess dural ectasia, spinal surgery and neurological symptoms if neuraxial analgesia is contemplated; dural ectasia can make spinal block unreliable and positioning difficult. Protect hypermobile joints, eyes and pressure areas.

### Conduct of anaesthesia
Use GA and a secured airway appropriate to the full-stomach/abdominal presentation. Plan airway technique and positioning from findings. Continue indicated rate/anti-impulse therapy unless haemodynamics contraindicate it; manage ARB according to indication and the agreed perioperative protocol. Avoid abrupt hypertension, tachycardia and marked contractility increases that raise aortic wall stress, while maintaining organ perfusion. An arterial line is reasonable with important aortopathy/valve disease or instability; choose access with known vascular anatomy in mind.

Pneumoperitoneum and head-up positioning can lower preload, increase afterload and CO2. Agree low pressure and gradual changes, maintain normocapnia and avoid excessive airway pressure, especially with bullae. Use titrated induction, analgesia and vasopressors rather than large abrupt cardiovascular changes. If significant AR coexists, **do not impose profound bradycardia blindly**: balance regurgitation/forward output with aortic protection with cardiology advice.

### Recovery
Smooth emergence, effective multimodal analgesia, respiratory and BP monitoring, surveillance for pneumothorax or dissection if new symptoms, careful antithrombotic restart and higher care according to aortic/valve severity. Ensure ongoing aortic surveillance and appropriate specialist follow-up.

items.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus requires urgent lower limb arterial bypass surgery. Their medications include dapagliflozin (a sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor). Outline your specific concerns and management of this patient for this procedure
items.model:
> **Source/examiner emphasis:** Balance limb urgency against SGLT2 cessation/optimisation; explain euDKA diagnosis and treatment, cardiovascular/renal vasculopathy and specific glucose monitoring rather than vague targets.

### Establish urgency and current physiology
Clarify acute versus chronic critical limb ischaemia and the harm of delaying bypass; discuss timing with the vascular surgeon. Review dapagliflozin last dose, fasting/intake, diabetes treatment, HbA1c if available, infection, dehydration, renal function and systemic atherosclerosis (CAD, stroke, HF). Assess ECG/symptoms, Hb, electrolytes, renal function and vascular/bleeding/antiplatelet plans. Do not delay a threatened limb merely to complete an elective drug interval.

### SGLT2-specific risk
Dapagliflozin promotes glycosuria and relative insulin/glucagon imbalance; fasting, stress and poor intake can precipitate **ketoacidosis despite near-normal glucose**. Stop it now. Check capillary blood beta-hydroxybutyrate, glucose and a venous/arterial gas with bicarbonate, pH and anion gap. Significant ketonaemia with high-anion-gap metabolic acidosis supports euDKA; exclude lactate, renal and other causes rather than diagnosing it from glucose alone. Use the current local SGLT2 emergency algorithm; a rising ketone level or illness prompts urgent gas/specialist review even before severe acidosis.

If euDKA is present, seek endocrine/ICU help, give monitored fluid resuscitation tailored to HF/renal reserve, IV insulin **with glucose/dextrose to permit suppression of ketogenesis**, K replacement/monitoring and treatment of the precipitant. Continue until ketosis/acidosis resolves, not merely until glucose is normal. If safe, stabilise before anaesthesia; genuinely life-saving surgery may require simultaneous treatment.

### Intraoperative and postoperative plan
Use frequent glucose measurements, for example hourly during IV insulin/major unstable surgery, with a local target commonly around **6–10 mmol/L** and avoidance of hypoglycaemia. Repeat ketones/gas/electrolytes according to recent exposure, risk and trajectory. Supply carbohydrate/insulin appropriately and minimise avoidable fasting. Titrate anaesthesia, maintain coronary and limb/renal perfusion, use appropriate invasive monitoring and replace measured loss without overloading a failing heart.

Plan monitored postoperative care, renal and limb checks and written diabetes/antiplatelet instructions. Restart dapagliflozin only after acute illness resolves, adequate oral intake and absence of ketosis. For subsequent elective procedures, prescribe the actual local last-dose schedule; AHA/ACC/FDA uses ≥72 h for this drug, while ANZ calendar schedules are distinct and bowel preparation may require earlier cessation.

items.q: Justify your perioperative management of the following medications in a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus scheduled for an elective laparotomy on a morning list: sodium-glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitor (SGLT2 inhibitor); glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1 receptor agonist); once-daily subcutaneous long-acting insulin.
items.model:
> **Source/examiner emphasis:** Question paper only: no examiner report was available in the checked archive at the audit cutoff. No examiner emphasis, pass rate or official allocation is invented.

### Shared assessment
Confirm agents/formulations, usual timing, HbA1c/glucose, renal function, hypoglycaemia, intake and anticipated postoperative fasting. Give written last-dose, monitoring and restart instructions. A morning laparotomy can have prolonged fasting; coordinate diabetes/anaesthetic teams and minimise avoidable delay.

### SGLT2 inhibitor
Withhold before elective major surgery under an explicit current local schedule because fasting/stress can cause **euglycaemic ketoacidosis**. AHA/ACC/FDA uses ≥72 h for dapa/empa/cana and ≥96 h for ertugliflozin; ANZ calendar-day rules differ. For a prolonged low-carbohydrate diet or bowel preparation, cessation may need to precede that phase. Recent use or illness requires blood ketones and gas/anion-gap assessment; normal glucose is not reassuring. Suspected euDKA needs specialist fluid/insulin plus dextrose/K treatment. Restart only when stable with normal intake and no ketosis.

### GLP-1 receptor agonist
ANZCA/ADS/GESA/NACOS 2025 recommends **continuation**, rather than routine cessation, with a 24-h clear-fluid diet and the specified subsequent fasting plan. Delayed gastric emptying increases retained-content/aspiration risk; absence of GI symptoms does not reliably exclude it and stopping a long-acting agent briefly may not normalise emptying. If diet/preparation is incomplete, use the local risk-mitigation pathway: appropriately trained gastric ultrasound, selected prokinetic assessment, delay when appropriate or full-stomach airway precautions. The ANZCA April 2026 clarification specifies water only from six hours and no intake for the final two hours under that pathway. Tailor carbohydrate/insulin advice during the clear-fluid period and postoperative restart/continuation to tolerance.

### Once-daily long-acting insulin
Provide basal insulin at an **adjusted dose**, rather than automatically withholding all insulin. Many elective type-2 pathways use around **80% of the usual basal dose**, with the exact evening/morning schedule determined by formulation, usual administration time, renal function and hypoglycaemia risk. Confirm the institutional diabetes chart. For long fasting/major surgery or poor control, plan IV insulin with glucose and electrolyte monitoring; continuation of an adjusted basal dose during IV treatment depends on the protocol. Insulin is essential in type 1 diabetes; although this stem is type 2, do not generalise an omission rule across diabetes types.

Check glucose on admission and regularly, often hourly with IV insulin or unstable major surgery; a common target is approximately 6–10 mmol/L with local acceptable range. Treat hypoglycaemia promptly, monitor K, and prescribe postoperative transition to subcutaneous/enteral treatment with reliable food intake and no insulin gap.

items.q: A 68-year-old man is scheduled for total knee replacement next week. He has hypertension, for which he is prescribed enalapril, and type 2 diabetes, for which he is prescribed metformin. Justify your perioperative management of his medications.
items.model:
> **Verified examiner emphasis:** Justify stopping versus continuing each agent using physiology, patient risk and a coherent perioperative plan; a memorised drug list is insufficient.

### Patient and operation
Confirm BP control, HF/CAD, renal function, electrolytes, glucose/HbA1c, hypoglycaemia history and other medicines. Total knee replacement may involve neuraxial sympathectomy, bleeding, fasting and postoperative renal/volume changes. Plan prescribing and restart, not simply a preoperative omission.

### Enalapril
ACE inhibition treats hypertension and may treat HF, but reduces angiotensin-mediated compensation during anaesthesia; continuation increases hypotension risk. Conversely, omission can worsen BP control and interrupt useful HF treatment. STOP-or-NOT found similar major postoperative outcomes with continuation versus withholding, with more intraoperative hypotension after continuation.

Current policies differ: AHA/ACC allows withholding approximately 24 h in selected hypertensive patients having elevated-risk surgery and favours continuation for compensated reduced-EF HF; AoA/BIHS 2026 generally continues ACEI/ARB. **For this hypertension-only patient, document the local protocol and actual last dose**; withholding is reasonable if important hypotension/neuraxial or volume risk is anticipated, but is not universally mandatory. If continued, prepare for hypotension rather than cancel automatically. Treat hypotension by cause, with fluid for genuine deficit and titrated vasopressors; refractory ACE-related vasoplegia may require vasopressin. Restart once perfusion, renal function and potassium permit, with a named prescriber.

### Metformin
Metformin rarely causes hypoglycaemia alone. Accumulation with AKI or hypoperfusion increases lactic-acidosis concern. Confirm renal function, acute illness, expected fasting, route/intake and any contrast exposure. There is no mandatory 48-h preoperative cessation for every well patient.

For a short elective pathway with stable renal function, some current guidance allows continuation. For anticipated major surgery with prolonged fasting or AKI/hypoperfusion risk, withholding on the day is a reasonable local strategy. Explain the choice rather than claim one universal rule. Monitor capillary glucose at agreed intervals and treat hyperglycaemia with a defined insulin protocol if needed; metformin omission alone does not mandate an insulin infusion. Resume when eating, clinically stable and renal function remains appropriate; after AKI or relevant contrast exposure use the renal/contrast-specific reassessment pathway.

### Whole perioperative plan
Avoid dehydration and excessive fasting, maintain perfusion, monitor glucose and electrolytes, review renal function if clinically indicated and provide clear discharge instructions. Do not initiate a high-dose beta-blocker purely to compensate for withholding enalapril. Ensure the surgical/ward team knows which drugs were omitted and why.

items.title: Landmark trials at a glance
items.body:
The following are the primary studies with the greatest direct influence on Set 18 anaesthetic decisions. A guideline or consensus is not mislabeled as a randomised trial. Read each study as population → treatment/comparator → outcome → implication and limits.

**T1 — PRESCRIPT (Buitenwerf et al., 2020): phenoxybenzamine versus doxazosin before phaeochromocytoma surgery.** [Original multicentre RCT](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31714582/). Among 134 patients with nonmetastatic pheochromocytoma/sympathetic paraganglioma, time outside target intraoperative BP range was **11.1% vs 12.2%** (not significantly different); a secondary haemodynamic instability score favoured phenoxybenzamine, but 30-day cardiovascular complications were not significantly different. **Lesson:** titrated alpha blockade and thoughtful volume/BP preparation matter more than declaring one agent universally outcome-superior. **Limitation:** comparatively small, open-label study; no definitive evidence on rare major cardiovascular outcomes.

**T2 — BEST-Fluids (Collins et al., Lancet 2023): low-chloride balanced crystalloid versus normal saline for deceased-donor kidney transplantation.** [Original randomised trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37343576/). A large multicentre ANZ kidney-transplant trial showed **reduced delayed graft function** with balanced crystalloid versus 0.9% saline. **Lesson:** prefer balanced low-chloride crystalloid as the default transplant fluid, while still individualising total volume, potassium and haemodynamic support. **Limitation:** deceased-donor transplants and trial-specific perioperative fluid strategy; not proof that every renal impairment or transplant recipient benefits from an arbitrary amount of crystalloid.

**T3 — RELIEF (Myles et al., NEJM 2018): restrictive versus liberal perioperative fluids in major abdominal surgery.** [Original RCT](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1801601). Approximately 3000 high-risk adults; disability-free survival at one year **81.9% restrictive vs 82.3% liberal** (no significant advantage), but **AKI 8.6% vs 5.0%** with the more restrictive regimen. **Lesson:** avoid both excessive crystalloid and inadequate organ perfusion; do not equate enhanced recovery with zero fluid. **Limitation:** studied particular protocols and higher-risk **major** abdominal surgery, not tiny ambulatory cases or every robotic procedure.

**T4 — NICE-SUGAR (2009): intensive versus conventional glucose targets in the ICU.** [Original trial](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0810625). In over 6100 critically ill adults, intensive targeting around 4.5–6.0 mmol/L increased 90-day mortality (**27.5% vs 24.9%**) and severe hypoglycaemia compared with a conventional less-intensive target. **Lesson:** in critically ill postoperative patients, avoid forcing tight normoglycaemia at the expense of hypoglycaemia. **Limitation:** ICU rather than all ambulatory operations; perioperative glucose ranges must be chosen according to clinical setting and guidance.

**T5 — Regional analgesia for breast surgery: contemporary comparative systematic evidence (2025).** [Cochrane network meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12135142/). Multiple regional techniques reduced postoperative pain/opioids versus no block, with limited clinically important superiority between individual techniques. **Lesson:** select PECS/pectoserratus, paravertebral, serratus or other regional technique according to **incision and actual nerve coverage** rather than one proclaimed universal “best” block. **Limitation:** this is a **systematic review, not one RCT**; heterogeneous procedures, techniques and endpoints.

**T6 — Modern carcinoid crisis management (2026 international Delphi consensus).** [Primary consensus publication](https://academic.oup.com/bjsopen/article/10/5/zrag159/9003020). The panel recommended **vasopressors as first-line treatment and octreotide only as an adjunct**; routine prophylactic bolus/infusion is not necessary. **Lesson:** update older octreotide-first algorithms. **Limitation:** this is expert consensus drawing on low-to-moderate quality evidence, not a definitive randomised comparison of crisis treatments. Its inclusion is intentional because it materially changes contemporary teaching.

items.title: Reading list and linked references
items.body:
## Evidence audit and scope

The workbook’s nine allocated rows are mapped below. Where a row is shared with other sets, the list reflects **only components explicitly marked for Set 18**. The priority is used to determine relative teaching depth rather than assuming every outcome deserves the same number of pages.

**Allocation check:** 9 LO codes, **5 complete rows / 4 component-only rows**. The workbook’s header states 48 explicit components; some appear as several nested bullets within one parent outcome. The notes have addressed every named worksheet component, but do **not** reclassify parent BT_PO 1.5 as fully completed in Set 18. SAQ bank mapping (listed in workbook) influenced emphasis only; the separate SAQ/Retrieve/Speak banks were not recreated or audited here.

## What a complete Final answer should contain

An **‘outline’** answer states the clinically material risk and a safe phase-specific strategy; it does not require a textbook chapter on molecular biochemistry. A **‘discuss’** answer adds mechanism, competing options and justification—for example, why use a direct vasoactive drug after phaeochromocytoma vein ligation, why saline vs balanced crystalloid differs in transplantation, or why awake spinal TURP may reveal irrigation absorption. A **‘specific anaesthetic management including fluids and analgesia’** answer names surgical phases, access/monitoring, airway/position, haemodynamic targets and their limitations, named fluid and analgesia options, rescue pathways and postoperative complications. These requirements were used to judge whether the notes go beyond a topic mention.

## Linked references and source register

**Clinical guidelines and specialty recommendations**

- **R1 — ACC/AHA (2024, reaffirmed) guideline for perioperative cardiovascular care.** [Primary guideline](https://www.jacc.org/doi/10.1016/j.jacc.2024.06.013). Use for perioperative medicine and explicit SGLT2 inhibitor withholding recommendations (3–4 days), cardiovascular stratification and medicines. Compare with UK guideline rather than merging contradictory timing.
- **R2 — 2025 multidisciplinary UK consensus on GLP-1, dual GIP–GLP-1 and SGLT2 inhibitors.** [Full peer-reviewed consensus](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11885194/). Use for aspiration-risk stratification, fasting/ketone mitigation and the UK shorter SGLT2 withholding approach; local NZ policies may differ.
- **R3 — ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes, Hospital Care (2025).** [Official guidance](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11635037/). Use for glucose target ≈5.6–10 mmol/L, perioperative insulin adjustment, avoiding hypoglycaemia, basal insulin and ketone vigilance.
- **R4 — Society for Obesity and Bariatric Anaesthesia best-practice airway recommendations (2025).** [Published recommendations](https://doi.org/10.1111/anae.16647). Directly useful for ramped ≥30° head-up preoxygenation, first-line videolaryngoscopy, apnoeic oxygenation and head-up awake extubation.
- **R5 — ESE/Endocrine Society 2024 guideline on glucocorticoid-induced adrenal insufficiency.** [Full guideline](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11180513/). Use for crisis recognition and parenteral perioperative stress coverage, with acknowledgement that lower-dose local protocols exist for selected minor/moderate procedures.
- **R8 — International expert consensus, perioperative carcinoid crisis (2026).** [Primary publication](https://academic.oup.com/bjsopen/article/10/5/zrag159/9003020). Mandatory current update for vasopressor-first versus historical octreotide-first teaching; echo screening for carcinoid heart disease.
- **R9 — American Thyroid Association guideline for thyrotoxicosis and thyroid storm (2016).** [Full primary guideline](https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/thy.2016.0229). Mechanism-based antithyroid, iodine, corticosteroid, rate control and ICU management. Its age does not invalidate core pathophysiology; adapt drug protocols to current local endocrinology practice.
- **R10 — British/European gynae endoscopy societies: hysteroscopy distension-fluid guideline.** [Full primary guidance](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5133285/). Essential for irrigant choice, deficit recording and stopping limits (hypotonic vs isotonic, reduced limits in comorbidity).
- **R14 — American Urological Association educational review of radical cystectomy perioperative optimisation and ERAS (2023).** [Specialty educational chapter](https://auau.auanet.org/sites/default/files/media/2023-11/Lesson%2037.pdf). Use for cystectomy-specific anaemia, nutrition, thromboembolism, fluid/analgesia, bowel recovery and stoma care.
- **R15 — NICE guideline on metastatic spinal cord compression (2023).** [Official recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng234/chapter/Recommendations). Use for urgent MRI, timely referral and dexamethasone where neurological symptoms occur.

**BJA Education, anaesthetic and transplant reviews (read alongside current guidance)**

- **R6 — BJA Education, Perioperative care of phaeochromocytoma (2016).** [Article](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/16/5/153/2389873). Strong for tumour physiology, alpha-before-beta blockade and the opposing haemodynamic phases; update individual drug warnings with contemporary specialist practice.
- **R7 — Pheochromocytoma Across the Perioperative Course: Current Concepts and Clinical Management (2026).** [Current clinical review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13624540/). Use for biochemical tests, perioperative optimisation, vasoactive choices and post-ligation risks.
- **R11 — Regional anaesthesia for breast cancer surgery: techniques and sensory coverage (2025).** [Narrative review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11920543/), plus [2025 network meta-analysis](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12135142/). Maps pectoral/intercostobrachial/parasternal contributions and block limitations.
- **R12 — Considerations regarding anesthesia for renal transplantation (2024).** [Anaesthetic review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10847005/). For preoperative ESRD assessment, anaesthetic drugs, renal perfusion, immunosuppression and postoperative assessment; drug protocols vary locally.
- **R13 — Perioperative considerations in kidney transplantation: an anaesthesiologist’s perspective (2025).** [Full review](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12679201/). Current broad overview of balanced crystalloids, reperfusion, monitoring, medications and analgesia. Note some fixed MAP/dose suggestions are centre-derived and not universal outcome thresholds.
- **R16 — Transplant/immunocompromised patient guidance (source of general principles).** [NICE neutropenic sepsis recommendations](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/cg151) for sepsis recognition/treatment in neutropenic patients; combine with the patient’s own organ-transplant team protocols and medication-specific interaction checking.

**Further relevant BJA Education and predecessor articles — what to read them for**

- **R17 — Wynn-Hebden A, Bouch DC. Anaesthesia for the obese patient (BJA Education, 2020).** [Full-text article](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7807945/). Best for obesity effects on FRC/oxygenation, OSA/OHS, drug dosing, preoxygenation and emergence; supplement its older recommendations with the 2025 SOBA airway guideline [R4].
- **R18 — Mayhew D et al. Update on the intraoperative management of adult cadaveric renal transplantation (BJA Education, 2016).** [Journal article](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/16/2/53/2897764). An especially useful operation-by-operation explanation of recipient optimisation, implantation/reperfusion, haemodynamics and immunosuppression. **Do not retain older routine saline/CVP/diuretic assumptions** against BEST-Fluids and contemporary transplant practice [T2,R13].
- **R19 — Anaesthesia for robot-assisted laparoscopic surgery (Continuing Education in Anaesthesia, Critical Care & Pain, 2009).** [Journal article](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/article-abstract/9/4/125/351594). Useful for why robotic docking, steep head-down positioning and CO₂ pneumoperitoneum require special airway/ventilation and emergency-access planning; supplement with contemporary robotic systems and obesity recommendations.
- **R20 — Morosan M, Popham P. Anaesthesia for gynaecological oncological surgery (Continuing Education in Anaesthesia, Critical Care & Pain, 2014).** [Journal issue/article record](https://academic.oup.com/bjaed/issue/14/2). Helps contextualise the extent of cytoreduction, surgical blood loss, fluid shifts, perioperative analgesia and postoperative organ support in major pelvic cancer surgery; supplement with modern ERAS and anticoagulant protocols.

**Core original trials and broader source material**

- **BEST-Fluids** [original Lancet trial record](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37343576/); **PRESCRIPT** [original trial](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/31714582/); **RELIEF** [original NEJM paper](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa1801601); **NICE-SUGAR** [original NEJM paper](https://www.nejm.org/doi/full/10.1056/NEJMoa0810625). Read the interpretations in Section 20 rather than memorising isolated percentages.
- **ANZCA training programme curriculum v1.14 (Appendix Five)** and **Prioritised LEarning Sets(5).xlsx** (Set 18 tab): definitive scope and priorities for these notes, supplied in this project. Cross-set curriculum rows are not silently reclassified here.
- **ANZCA Final Examination Chairs’ Reports 2020–2026**, supplied in the project: useful for expected clinical decision depth (phaeochromocytoma 2023.1 and 2026.1; post-heart-transplant patient 2025.1; hysteroscopy 2023.2; obesity/robotics 2025.1; thyroidectomy 2023.2; renal transplantation 2022.2). These illustrate examiner emphasis and are not treated as an exhaustive future-topic prediction.
- **R21 —** [ERAS Society guideline for gynaecologic oncology: 2026 update](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.ygyno.2026.05.022). Current specialty guidance on open versus minimally invasive gynaecological oncological surgery, goal-directed fluids, multimodal regional analgesia, extubation and functional recovery. Used for the surgical and fast-track expansions.
- **R22 —** [Association of Anaesthetists / Joint British Diabetes Societies perioperative diabetes consensus (2026)](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC13352544/). Current care-planning, capillary glucose targets, IV insulin monitoring and transitions of care. Regional recommendations may differ from Australasian local protocols; use with existing R1–R3.

**Verification limitations.** The set is a curriculum-mapped teaching synthesis using current accessible primary guidance/trials and peer-reviewed reviews. Some source pages give an abstract or guideline summary rather than a fully reviewed proprietary textbook chapter. Recommendations for immunosuppressant timing, renal transplant target MAP, hydrocortisone dose in minor surgery, GLP-1 medication management and vasoactive doses may differ by specialty centre; these are explicitly presented as context-dependent. No copyrighted textbook prose or charts are reproduced; the diagrams are original teaching schematics.
